title: Week 2 | Day 2
text:
0. Motivation & Yesterday
Yesterday: spatial coverages (grid, hexagon, Voronoi, Delaunay) — algorithms to partition and interpolate space.
Today: interactive visualization — how to publish so others explore without coding.
Why? Your analysis is only useful if stakeholders (water managers, EPA, public) can interact with it. This requires understanding web constraints: tiles, projections, performance.

title: Week 2 | Day 2
text:
Learning Objectives

Understand the CRS constraint for web maps: all interactive web mapping uses WGS84 (EPSG:4326).
Know when to use Leaflet (simple, familiar), WebGL (GPU, 10k+ points), vs. vector tiles (100k+, complex styling).
Build interactive leaflet maps with markers, popups, clustering, and layers.
Produce and serve vector tiles (.pmtiles, .mbtiles) for large datasets.
Author map styles using freestiler → Mapbox/MapLibre JSON for tile-based maps.

title: Week 2 | Day 2
text:
1. What is Leaflet?
Leaflet — open-source JavaScript library for interactive web maps.
Used by: New York Times, Washington Post, GitHub, OpenStreetMap, Mapbox, CartoDB, USGS, EPA.
Why Leaflet (not ArcGIS Online, Mapbox Studio, etc.)?

Simple: Layer-by-layer like ggplot2
R native: leaflet package — build maps in R code
Flexible: Works in Rmd, Quarto, Shiny, plain HTML
Free: No subscriptions, no API keys for basemaps
Fast: Optimized for panning/zooming on mobile
Plugins: 100+ extensions (clustering, 3D, heatmaps, etc.)

title: Week 2 | Day 2
text:
2. Why Build Maps in R?
Maps should be reproducible, version-controlled, scriptable — like all your code.
R advantages: - Maps are code (git-tracked, shareable) - Embed directly in reports (Rmd, Quarto) - Automated updates — rerun code, map updates - Consistency — same CRS handling, styling across all maps - Scalability — generate 100 maps from a loop
ArcGIS drawbacks for research: - Click-based (hard to reproduce) - Saved as .mxd (proprietary, hard to version) - Sharing requires purchase or web license - Updates are manual reclicks

title: Week 2 | Day 2
text:
3. Map Building Blocks (Like ggplot2)

leaflet() |>                                # Initialize
  addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB) |>   # Basemap tile layer
  addCircleMarkers(data = sites) |>        # Data points (sf object)
  addPolylines(data = rivers, color = ...) # Lines
  addPolygons(data = zones) |>             # Polygons (with fill)
  setView(lng = -105, lat = 40, zoom = 10) # Set center & zoom

Components: - Basemaps: CartoDB, OpenStreetMap, Satellite, Imagery, Terrain - Markers: pins (circles, awesomeIcons, custom images) - Shapes: polylines (rivers, roads), polygons (watersheds, zoning), rectangles - Interactive: Popups (click), labels (hover), clustering, heatmaps - UI: Legend, scale bar, search, draw tools, fullscreen

title: Week 2 | Day 2
section: 4. The CRS Constraint: Web Maps Are Always 4326
text:
4. The CRS Constraint: Web Maps Are Always 4326
You learned EPSG:5070 for analysis (equal-area, no distortion).
Web browsers have no choice: all maps use WGS84 (EPSG:4326).
Why? Web tiles are pre-rendered globally in a Mercator grid. Only works in 4326.
The workflow:

## 1. Analyze in EPSG:5070 (accurate areas, distances)
watersheds <- st_read("shp") |> st_transform(5070) |> 
  mutate(area_km2 = drop_units(st_area(.) / 1e6))

## 2. Transform to 4326 ONLY when publishing to web
watersheds_web <- watersheds |> st_transform(4326)

## 3. Map it
leaflet(watersheds_web) |> addPolygons(color = ~color_by_area(area_km2))

This is the ONLY time you transform away from your analysis CRS.

title: Week 2 | Day 2
section: 5. Map Tiles: A Tiled Web Map (Slippy Map)
text:
5. Map Tiles: A Tiled Web Map (Slippy Map)
A tiled web map seamlessly joins dozens of 256×256 pixel images streamed over the internet.
Google Maps conventions (adopted industry-wide):

Each tile is exactly 256 pixels × 256 pixels
At zoom level 0, the entire world fits in one 256px tile
Each zoom level doubles in both X and Y → replaces 1 tile with 4
About 22 zoom levels are sufficient for Earth to building-level detail
Web Mercator projection (EPSG:3857) is standard — includes latitude limits at approximately ±85°

OpenStreetMap “Slippy Map” standard:

URL format: http://.../{Z}/{X}/{Y}.png

Z = zoom level (0–22)
X = column index (0 at left, increases rightward)
Y = row index (0 at top, increases downward)

All tiles are PNG images
Worldwide coverage at all zoom levels

title: Week 2 | Day 2
text:
6. Zoom Levels & Tile Coordinates
At zoom 0, the entire Earth is one 256×256 pixel tile. As you zoom in, tiles split exponentially:

Zoom 0: 1 tile (1×1 grid)
Zoom 1: 4 tiles (2×2 grid)
Zoom Z: \(4^Z\) tiles total

At zoom 18 (street-level), there are ~68 billion tiles covering Earth.
Tile coordinates & URLs:
Tiles are indexed by (Z, X, Y) with (0,0) at top-left:
https://tile-server.org/{Z}/{X}/{Y}.png
Example: UCSB at zoom 18
https://a.tile.openstreetmap.org/18/43803/104352.png

Tile column 43803, row 104352 → PNG of UCSB streets
Each pixel ≈ 1.2 meters on the ground

Key insight: Each zoom increments X/Y quadrants, so user pans/zooms seamlessly fetch neighboring tiles client-side.

title: Week 2 | Day 2
text:
7. Tile Size & Resolution Math
The horizontal distance covered by each tile depends on latitude and zoom level:
\[S_{tile} = C \cdot \cos(latitude) / 2^{zoomlevel}\]
where \(C = 2\pi \cdot 6,378,137\) m (Earth’s equatorial circumference).
One pixel in that tile represents:
\[S_{pixel} = S_{tile} / 256\]
Example: UCSB (lat = 34.414°, zoom = 18)

C <- 2 * pi * 6378137.00
S_tile <- C * cos(34.4140 * pi / 180) / 2^18
S_pixel <- S_tile / 256

cat("Tile covers:", round(S_tile), "meters\n")
cat("Each pixel:", round(S_pixel, 2), "meters\n")

At zoom 18, each pixel is roughly 1.2 meters on the ground — street-level detail.

title: Week 2 | Day 2
text:
8. Web Mercator Projection & Distortion
All web tiles use Web Mercator (EPSG:3857), a cylinder projection that:

Preserves shapes locally (locally conformal) — good for navigation
Severely distorts high latitudes — Greenland looks huge, Antarctica is cut off
Latitude limits at ±85° — mathematically, Mercator is undefined at ±90°

Why the distortion?
Mercator inflates distances north-south exponentially with latitude:
\[y = \ln(\tan(\pi/4 + \text{lat}/2))\]

Equator: 256 pixels ≈ 40,000 km (accurate)
60° latitude: same 256 pixels ≈ 20,000 km (stretched 2×)
Greenland (70°): drags to continent size despite being 1/14th of Africa







Important


Web Mercator distorts areas, angles, and distances. Never use it for analysis. Use EPSG:5070 (equal-area), UTM (equidistant), or other appropriate CRS for all calculations. Transform to 4326 only at publication.

title: Week 2 | Day 2
section: 9. User Zooming: The Pyramid in Action
text:
9. User Zooming: The Pyramid in Action
When a user zooms in:

Browser requests 4 new tiles to replace the 1 parent tile
New tiles are at zoom level Z+1 with finer detail
Process repeats smoothly — pan, pinch, scroll wheel

When a user zooms out:

Browser requests 1 coarser parent tile (zoom level Z-1)
Old 4 tiles are discarded
Map simplifies smoothly

Result: Users experience seamless, fast panning/zooming because: - Only visible tiles download - Pre-rendered tiles are cached on CDNs - Browser memory is minimal (a few MB of tiles at a time)

title: Week 2 | Day 2
text:
10. Leaflet in R: Why & How
Leaflet is built in JavaScript, but the R package leaflet makes it easy:

Write pure R code — no JavaScript knowledge needed
Works in Rmd, Quarto, Shiny, RStudio Viewer
Maps become interactive HTML objects
Compatible with sf simple features — pass sf objects directly

Building blocks (like ggplot2):

library(leaflet)

leaflet(data) |>                    # Initialize
  addProviderTiles(providers$...) |> # Add basemap
  addMarkers(popup = ~name) |>       # Add markers
  addPolygons(color = ~color) |>     # Add shapes
  setView(lng, lat, zoom)            # Set center

text:
15. Demo: Earthquakes with Clustering


Code:

library(leaflet); library(sf)

quakes_sf <- quakes |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("long", "lat"), 
           crs = 4326)

leaflet(quakes_sf) |>
  addProviderTiles(
    providers$CartoDB.Positron
  ) |>
  addCircleMarkers(
    radius = ~pmin(8, mag),
    color = ~colorFactor(
      "RdYlBu", NULL)(mag),
    stroke = FALSE,
    fillOpacity = 0.6,
    popup = ~paste0(
      "Mag: ", mag, 
      " | Depth: ", depth),
    clusterOptions = 
      markerClusterOptions()
  ) |>
  setView(180, -20, zoom = 3)


Interactive map: Click clusters to zoom and drill down

title: Week 2 | Day 2
text:
16. Why Clustering? Performance & UX
Clustering benefits:

Reduces clutter — 5k points become 5–10 clusters initially
Enables drill-down — click clusters to zoom and see child points
Server-side pre-computation — R calculates once, sends static GeoJSON
Fast at all zoom levels — Leaflet handles aggregation client-side

When to use:

✅ 5k–20k points, interactive exploration
✅ Users browse hierarchically (zoom-in behavior)
❌ 100k+ points (too slow even with clustering; use WebGL or vector tiles)
❌ Real-time streaming (server-side clustering is static)

Tool
Approach
Sweet Spot
Trade-off

title: Week 2 | Day 2

text:
24. Vector Tiles & Styling with freestiler
Why vector tiles: client requests small tiles of vector data and applies style client-side — massive datasets become browsable.
Pipeline overview:

Prepare GeoJSON or NDJSON.
Create .mbtiles using tippecanoe (OS-level tool).
Optionally convert .mbtiles → .pmtiles for a single portable file.
Author style JSON using freestiler (R) to produce Mapbox/MapLibre style JSON.
Serve .pmtiles via static hosting or pmtiles-aware server and point MapLibre/Mapbox/leaflet-mapbox-gl.js at the tile endpoint.

Commands (guide only):
# make mbtiles
tippecanoe -o cities.mbtiles -Z0 -z14 data/cities.geojson

# convert to pmtiles (requires pmtiles CLI or Python tool)
pmtiles convert cities.mbtiles cities.pmtiles

# serve with a static file server (development)
python -m http.server 8000
freestiler (R) example: produce a Mapbox-style JSON from R objects

library(freestiler)
# create a basic style and write to file
style <- freestiler::freestile() |> 
  add_background("#fff") |> 
  add_vector_layer(source = "cities", paint = list("circle-color" = "#1f78b4"))
writeLines(jsonlite::toJSON(style, auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE), "style.json")

Client side: MapLibre or mapbox-gl in the browser reads style.json and tiles endpoint.
Notes: mapdeck uses deck.gl; for production without Mapbox, serve styles via MapLibre + pmtiles host.

WMS Tiles & Real-time Data:

library(leaflet)

# WMS = Web Map Service (pre-rendered images)
# NEXRAD = live weather radar

conus <- filter(us_states(), !stusps %in% c("AK", "PR", "HI"))

leaflet() |>

  addPolygons(

    fillColor = "transparent",
    color = "black", weight = 1

  addWMSTiles(
    "https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/cgi-bin/wms/nexrad/n0r.cgi",

    )

title: Week 2 | Day 2
Week 2 | Day 2
text:
24. Vector Tiles & PMTiles
Vector tiles: GeoJSON delivered at tile level—styling happens client-side (1M+ features, 10–100× smaller files than raster).
Quick pipeline:
# 1. Create tiles from GeoJSON
tippecanoe -o data.mbtiles -Z0 -z14 data.geojson

# 2. Convert to PMTiles (single portable file)
pmtiles convert data.mbtiles data.pmtiles

# 3. Serve via static host or Python
python -m http.server 8000
In R with freestiler (style authoring):

library(freestiler)

style <- freestile() |>
  add_background("#fff") |>
  add_vector_layer(
    source = "cities",
    type = "circle",
    paint = list("circle-color" = "#1f77b4", "circle-radius" = 5)
  )

jsonlite::write_json(style, "style.json", auto_unbox = TRUE)

Why PMTiles? Single file, HTTP range requests, portable—host on GitHub Pages or static CDN.

5. Theme

Great! Now we just need to polish our plots…
ggplot offers a themeing system:

elements specify the non-data elements that you can control. For example,


plot.title controls the appearance of the plot title;
axis.ticks.x controls the ticks on the x axis;
legend.key.height, controls the height of the keys in the legend.


Each element is associated with an element function, which describes the visual properties. For example,


element_text() sets the font size, color and face of text elements like plot.title.


The theme() function which allows you to override default elements:


For example theme(plot.title = element_text(color = "red")).

title: Week 2
text:
From Tabular to Spatial
Last week: data as rows and columns — wrangling, joining, visualizing, modeling.

This week: data as features in space — the same verbs, but now every observation has a geometry that describes where it is and what shape it takes.


Today’s arc:

Simple Features — the standard and the R implementation
Spatial Computing: The Stack — GDAL, PROJ, GEOS (the C++ libraries under sf)
Coordinate Systems — GCS, datums, projections
Measurements — distance, area, units

(We’ll take a 5-minute break after Simple Features.)

title: Week 2
section: Why CRS Matters for Water Resources
text:
Why CRS Matters for Water Resources
Before we start: the single most common silent error in spatial water resources analysis.


USGS NWIS gauge coordinates → WGS84 (EPSG:4326)
NHDPlus HR flowlines → NAD83 (EPSG:4269)

3DEP elevation → varies by tile



These are different coordinate systems. The differences are small (~1–3 meters for NAD83 vs. WGS84) but:

Joining gauges to their catchments? Wrong
Snapping gauges to the nearest flowline? Wrong
Computing distance from a gauge to a dam? Wrong









Important


Always check CRS before any spatial join or distance calculation. We’ll learn the three tools that make this automatic.

title: Week 2
section: Why Classes Matter: One Data Structure, Many Behaviors
text:
Why Classes Matter: One Data Structure, Many Behaviors
You’ve already used S3 classes in tidyverse without noticing. The same object type can behave differently based on its class.
Understanding S3 classes in R explains:

Why print() on a tibble looks different than a regular data.frame



Why filter() on grouped data filters within each group instead of globally




Why summarize() on a grouped_df produces a different output shape



This is the callback pattern — R looks at an object’s class and dispatches to the right function. Later, sf will extend data.frame with spatial methods that work the same way.

title: Week 2
text:
Adding Class: Matrix → Data Frame
A class is metadata attached to an object telling R how to interpret and operate on it:

# Start with a matrix — just numbers in rows and columns
v <- c(1,2,3,4,5,6)
class(v)
#> [1] "numeric"
m <- matrix(v, nrow = 3)
class(m)
#> [1] "matrix" "array"
m
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    1    4
#> [2,]    2    5
#> [3,]    3    6


# Add class metadata: "this is a data frame"
df <- as.data.frame(m)
class(df)
#> [1] "data.frame"
df
#>   V1 V2
#> 1  1  4
#> 2  2  5
#> 3  3  6

Same data. But now df has column names, printed summary, and methods that respect rectangular structure. The class changed the behavior without changing the underlying values.

title: Week 2
text:
Class Hierarchies: Adding Layers
Objects can have multiple classes in a hierarchy. Adding structure adds more classes:

# Plain data.frame
df <- data.frame(gauge = c("A", "B", "C"), flow = c(100, 120, 95))
class(df)
#> [1] "data.frame"

# Add grouping — now it has *two* classes
gdf <- group_by(df, gauge)
class(gdf)
#> [1] "grouped_df" "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"

# Methods are dispatched: dplyr functions check for "grouped_df" first
slice(gdf, 1)  # respects grouping — one row per group, not one global row
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#> # Groups:   gauge [3]
#>   gauge  flow
#>   <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 A       100
#> 2 B       120
#> 3 C        95
slice(df, 1)   # no grouping — just one row total
#>   gauge flow
#> 1     A  100


The key insight: the same function behaves differently based on class. This is the callback mechanism. When you call slice(), R internally asks: “What class is this object?” and dispatches to the right implementation.

title: Week 2
section: Methods: Functions That Know Their Object’s Class
text:
Methods: Functions That Know Their Object’s Class
Every function that respects class has methods or versions specialized for each class:

# Base R example: print() has different methods
print.data.frame()   # specialized for data.frames
print.default()      # fallback for other objects

# You can list all methods for a class:
methods(class = "data.frame")   # all functions with .data.frame versions


select(), filter(), mutate() are dplyr verbs that have methods:

methods("filter")    # shows filter.data.frame, filter.grouped_df, filter.ts, etc.
#> [1] filter.data.frame* filter.sf*         filter.ts*        
#> see '?methods' for accessing help and source code

title: Week 2
text:
The Dependencies Under sf
sf is powerful because it’s not built from scratch — it wraps three long standing C/C++ libraries, each with a focused job:

title: Week 2
text:
The Spatial Stack
Your R code:
sf::st_read("data.shp")      # I/O
sf::st_distance(a, b)        # Geometry
sf::st_transform(x, 4269)    # CRS








📦 GDAL


File I/O

Format translators
Reads/writes Shapefile, GeoJSON, GeoPackage, GeoTIFF
Returns WKB geometry











🧭 PROJ


Coordinate Systems

Transforms between 10,000+ CRS definitions
Handles datum shifts & projections
Underlies st_transform()











⚙️ GEOS


Geometry Ops

Intersection, union, buffer, centroid
Distance calculations
Spatial predicates (st_intersects())

title: Week 2
text:
Why This Matters
Each library solves a hard problem:








Library
Solves
Water Resources Example




GDAL
“How do I read a shapefile or GeoPackage?”
Read NHD flowlines, USGS boundaries, stream gauges


PROJ
“How do I convert WGS84 to Albers?”
Transform NWIS gauges from GPS coordinates to federal projection


GEOS
“Is this point inside this polygon? What’s the distance?”
Snap gauge to nearest flowline, clip to basin



If we had to write these from scratch in R, it would take years. Instead, spatial computing in R benefits from decades of work by the OSGeo community.

title: Week 2
text:
The sf Wrapper

sf::sf_extSoftVersion()
#>           GEOS           GDAL         proj.4 GDAL_with_GEOS     USE_PROJ_H 
#>       "3.14.1"       "3.12.2"        "9.7.1"         "true"         "true" 
#>           PROJ 
#>        "9.7.1"

sf doesn’t reinvent these wheels. It:

Calls GDAL for I/O (st_read(), st_write())
Calls PROJ for CRS transformations (st_transform())
Calls GEOS for geometry operations (st_distance(), st_buffer(), spatial predicates)
Wraps results with S3 classes and methods so dplyr verbs (filter(), mutate(), select()) just work — same as tidyverse

This diagram shows the relationship: sf methods dispatch to GEOS for the heavy lifting, then return R objects.






Note


When you install the sf package on your machine, the R package manager compiles and links against GDAL, PROJ, and GEOS. If installation fails, it’s usually because one of these C/C++ libraries is missing from your system. This is why setting up spatial computing can be more complex than installing a pure-R package.

title: Week 2
text:
What Is a Simple Feature?

Simple features (ISO 19125-1:2004) is a standard describing how real-world objects can be represented in computers, with emphasis on their spatial geometry
It defines:

A class hierarchy of geometry types
A set of operations on those geometries
Binary and text encodings for storage and transfer




Widely implemented: PostGIS, ESRI ArcGIS, GDAL, GeoJSON — and sf in R
A subset of simple features (the big 7) forms the GeoJSON specification

title: Week 2
text:
What Is a Feature?
A feature is a thing in the real world — a river, a gauge, a watershed, a county.

Features often consist of other features:

A river system → a river → an outlet point
A watershed → sub-basins → individual reaches



The standard says: “A simple feature has both spatial and non-spatial attributes. Spatial attributes are geometry valued.”

The geometry describes where the feature is and how it is represented
A river’s geometry could be its watershed polygon, its mainstem linestring, or its outlet point — depending on the question




str(co)
#> Classes 'sf' and 'data.frame':   64 obs. of  5 variables:
#>  $ geoid   : chr  "08001" "08003" "08005" "08007" ...
#>  $ name    : chr  "Adams" "Alamosa" "Arapahoe" "Archuleta" ...
#>  $ aland   : num  3.02e+09 1.87e+09 2.07e+09 3.50e+09 6.62e+09 ...
#>  $ state_nm: chr  "Colorado" "Colorado" "Colorado" "Colorado" ...
#>  $ geometry:sfc_MULTIPOLYGON of length 64; first list element: List of 1
#>   ..$ :List of 1
#>   .. ..$ : num [1:132, 1:2] -105 -105 -105 -105 -105 ...
#>   ..- attr(*, "class")= chr [1:3] "XY" "MULTIPOLYGON" "sfg"
#>  - attr(*, "sf_column")= chr "geometry"
#>  - attr(*, "agr")= Factor w/ 3 levels "constant","aggregate",..: NA NA NA NA
#>   ..- attr(*, "names")= chr [1:4] "geoid" "name" "aland" "state_nm"

title: Week 2
text:
The Big 7 Geometry Types








Single
Description




POINT
Zero-dimensional — a single coordinate pair


LINESTRING
Sequence of points connected by straight line pieces — 1D


POLYGON
Closed ring with positive area — 2D; may have interior holes






Multi (same type)
Description




MULTIPOINT
Set of points


MULTILINESTRING
Set of linestrings


MULTIPOLYGON
Set of polygons






Mixed
Description




GEOMETRYCOLLECTION
Set of geometries of any type










Note


These 7 types cover virtually everything in water resources work: gauge locations (POINT), stream reaches (LINESTRING), watershed boundaries (POLYGON), and their multi-feature equivalents.

title: Week 2
text:
Dimensions
All geometries are composed of points defined in 2-, 3-, or 4-D space:

XY — standard 2D coordinates (longitude, latitude or easting, northing)
XYZ — adds altitude (elevation of stream bed, DEM surface)
XYM — adds a measure attribute independent of the feature (e.g., streamflow at a vertex — rarely used)
XYZM — both Z and M


Note: “dimension” here means coordinate dimension (XY vs XYZ), not whether the geometry has length or area:

m1 <- rbind(c(8,1), c(2,5), c(3,2))
st_dimension(st_multipoint(m1))    # 0 — point set, no length
#> [1] 0
st_dimension(st_linestring(m1))    # 1 — has length, no area
#> [1] 1

title: Week 2
text:
Valid Geometries
Rules for valid geometries:

LINESTRING — no self-intersections
POLYGON — rings must be closed
POLYGON — holes inside exterior only
POLYGON — rings touch at points only
POLYGON — no repeated paths







Warning


Run st_is_valid() to check your data. Fix invalid geometries with st_make_valid().

title: Week 2
text:
Empty Geometries
EMPTY geometries serve as “NA” placeholders for geometry types — they arise naturally from spatial operations:

(e <- st_intersection(st_point(c(0,0)), st_point(c(1,1))))
#> GEOMETRYCOLLECTION EMPTY
st_is_empty(e)
#> [1] TRUE

plot(st_point(c(0,0)), pch = 16)
plot(st_point(c(1,1)), add = TRUE, col = 'red', pch = 16)

title: Week 2
text:
Well-Known Text and Well-Known Binary
The simple feature standard defines two encodings:
Well-Known Text (WKT) — human-readable:

x <- st_linestring(matrix(10:1, 5))
st_as_text(x)
#> [1] "LINESTRING (10 5, 9 4, 8 3, 7 2, 6 1)"

LINESTRING = type · parentheses contain points · points separated by commas · coordinates separated by spaces

Well-Known Binary (WKB) — machine-readable, fast, lossless:

st_as_binary(x)
#>  [1] 01 02 00 00 00 05 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 24 40 00 00 00 00 00 00 14 40
#> [26] 00 00 00 00 00 00 22 40 00 00 00 00 00 00 10 40 00 00 00 00 00 00 20 40 00
#> [51] 00 00 00 00 00 08 40 00 00 00 00 00 00 1c 40 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 40 00 00
#> [76] 00 00 00 00 18 40 00 00 00 00 00 00 f0 3f

WKB is used to communicate with external libraries (GDAL, GEOS) and spatial databases. Converting back to R:

st_as_sfc("LINESTRING(10 5, 9 4, 8 3, 7 2, 6 1)")[[1]]
#> LINESTRING (10 5, 9 4, 8 3, 7 2, 6 1)

title: Week 2
text:
Three Classes, One Object


🟢 sf — a data.frame with feature attributes and a geometry column (class: sf)
🔴 sfc — the geometry list-column (set of geometries)
🔵 sfg — individual simple feature geometry (one geometry per feature)








Important


This is the S3 class hierarchy in action. sf is a subclass of data.frame adding the geometry column and specialized methods. When you call filter() on an sf object, R looks at its class and dispatches to the spatial-aware filter.sf() method, which respects the geometry column. Same pattern as grouped_df from tidyverse.

title: Week 2
text:
sfg: Simple Feature Geometry
sfg objects carry the geometry for a single feature. Storage rules:

A single POINT → numeric vector
Points in a LINESTRING or POLYGON ring → matrix (each row = a point)
Any other set → list


Creator functions (rarely used in practice — you usually read existing data):

(x <- st_point(c(1, 2)))
str(x)
#>  'XY' num [1:2] 1 2

(x <- st_linestring(matrix(c(1,2,3,4), ncol = 2)))
str(x)
#>  'XY' num [1:2, 1:2] 1 2 3 4

title: Week 2
text:
sfg: Class Structure
All geometry objects have an S3 class indicating (1) dimension, (2) type, (3) superclass:

(pt  <- st_point(c(0, 1)))
attributes(pt)
#> $class
#> [1] "XY"    "POINT" "sfg"

(pt2 <- st_point(c(0, 1, 4)))   # XYZ
attributes(pt2)
#> $class
#> [1] "XYZ"   "POINT" "sfg"

title: Week 2
text:
sfg: Same Points, Different Meaning
The same coordinate matrix creates geometries with entirely different dimensionality:

m1 <- rbind(c(8,1), c(2,5), c(3,2))

(mp <- st_multipoint(m1))   # zero-dimensional point set
(ls <- st_linestring(m1))   # one-dimensional line

st_dimension(mp); st_length(mp)
#> [1] 0
#> [1] 0
st_dimension(ls); st_length(ls)
#> [1] 1
#> [1] 10.37338

title: Week 2
text:
Mixed Geometries and GEOMETRYCOLLECTION
Sets of features can have heterogeneous geometry types — type becomes GEOMETRY:



(g <- st_sfc(st_point(c(0,0)),
             st_linestring(rbind(c(0,0), c(1,1)))))
#> Geometry set for 2 features 
#> Geometry type: GEOMETRY
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: 0 ymin: 0 xmax: 1 ymax: 1
#> CRS:           NA


Filter by type with st_is:

g |> st_is("LINESTRING")
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE

st_sf(geometry = g) |>
  filter(st_is(geometry, "LINESTRING"))
#> Simple feature collection with 1 feature and 0 fields
#> Geometry type: LINESTRING
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: 0 ymin: 0 xmax: 1 ymax: 1
#> CRS:           NA
#>                geometry
#> 1 LINESTRING (0 0, 1 1)



When intersections produce mixed types, use GEOMETRYCOLLECTION and extract:

pt   <- st_point(c(1,0))
ls   <- st_linestring(matrix(c(4,3,0,0), ncol=2))
poly <- st_polygon(list(matrix(c(5.5,7,7,6,5.5,0,0,-0.5,-0.5,0), ncol=2)))
j    <- st_geometrycollection(list(pt, ls, poly))

st_collection_extract(j, "POLYGON")

title: Week 2
text:
Conversion Between Types: st_cast

(co1   <- filter(co, name == "Larimer")$geometry)
#> Geometry set for 1 feature 
#> Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: -106.1954 ymin: 40.25778 xmax: -104.9431 ymax: 40.99844
#> Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84
(co_ls <- st_cast(co1, "MULTILINESTRING"))
#> Geometry set for 1 feature 
#> Geometry type: MULTILINESTRING
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: -106.1954 ymin: 40.25778 xmax: -104.9431 ymax: 40.99844
#> Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84

title: Week 2
text:
Casting: Feature vs. Set Level
Casting operates at the feature level, not the set level:

rbind(c(0,0), c(1,1), c(1,0), c(0,1)) |>
  st_linestring() |>
  st_cast("POINT")   # ⚠️ converts ONE line to ONE point — not what you want
#> Warning in st_cast.LINESTRING(st_linestring(rbind(c(0, 0), c(1, 1), c(1, :
#> point from first coordinate only
#> POINT (0 0)


To extract individual points, work at the set level (sfc):

(p <- rbind(c(0,0), c(1,1), c(1,0), c(0,1)) |>
   st_linestring() |>
   st_sfc() |>           # create a SET of one geometry
   st_cast("POINT"))     # now produces 4 individual points
#> Geometry set for 4 features 
#> Geometry type: POINT
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: 0 ymin: 0 xmax: 1 ymax: 1
#> CRS:           NA

title: Week 2
Week 2
text:
Sets of geometries



rbind(c(0,0), c(1,1), c(1,0), c(0,1)) |>
  st_linestring() |>
  st_sfc()



#> Geometry set for 1 feature 
#> Geometry type: LINESTRING
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: 0 ymin: 0 xmax: 1 ymax: 1
#> CRS:           NA

title: Week 2
Week 2
Week 2
text:
sfc: Geometry List-Columns
st_sfc creates sets of geometries — what becomes the sticky list-column in sf objects:

(sfc <- st_sfc(st_point(c(0,1)), st_point(c(-3,2))))
#> Geometry set for 2 features 
#> Geometry type: POINT
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: -3 ymin: 1 xmax: 0 ymax: 2
#> CRS:           NA
class(sfc)
#> [1] "sfc_POINT" "sfc"
attributes(sfc) |> names()
#> [1] "class"     "precision" "bbox"      "crs"       "n_empty"

The sfc object records for the whole set: precision, bounding box, CRS, and count of empty geometries.

title: Week 2
text:
Combine vs. Union
Combining geometries preserves interior boundaries. Unioning dissolves them.



(co_c <- st_combine(co$geometry))
#> Geometry set for 1 feature 
#> Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: -109.0602 ymin: 36.99246 xmax: -102.0415 ymax: 41.00342
#> Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84












(co_u <- st_union(co$geometry))
#> Geometry set for 1 feature 
#> Geometry type: POLYGON
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: -109.0602 ymin: 36.99246 xmax: -102.0415 ymax: 41.00342
#> Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84

title: Week 2
text:
Combine + Cast: Borders as Lines

co_c_ml <- st_combine(co$geometry) |> st_cast("MULTILINESTRING")
co_u_ml <- st_union(co$geometry)   |> st_cast("MULTILINESTRING")









Tip


This distinction matters constantly in water resources: county boundaries vs. watershed boundaries, stream reaches vs. the river network, individual gauge catchments vs. the basin outline.

title: Week 2
text:
CONUS: Combine vs. Union

us_c_ml <- st_combine(conus) |> st_cast("MULTILINESTRING")
us_u_ml <- st_union(conus)   |> st_cast("MULTILINESTRING")

title: Week 2

Simple Features: What You’ve Learned
You now understand:

The seven geometry types — POINT, LINESTRING, POLYGON, and their multi-equivalents
The class hierarchy — sfg (individual geometry) → sfc (set) → sf (dataframe with sticky geometry)
Valid geometries — self-intersecting lines and invalid polygons break spatial operations silently

Sticky geometry in dplyr — sf objects work naturally with pipes, filters, and ggplot

Now a 5-minute break, then: What makes these coordinates actually spatial? We’ll cover the Coordinate Reference System — the foundation that anchors every spatial operation.

title: Week 2
text:
5 Minutes
Back in 5. Next: coordinate systems, projections, and the three-part system (ellipsoid, datum, prime meridian) that determines whether your spatial analysis is correct or silently wrong.

title: Week 2
text:
What Makes Spatial Data Spatial?

The geometry alone is meaningless without knowing where on Earth those coordinates refer to. That’s the job of the Coordinate Reference System.

title: Week 2
text:
Coordinate Reference Systems
A Coordinate Reference System (CRS) defines how spatial features relate to the surface of the Earth.
Two broad types:

Geographic Coordinate System (GCS) — locations on the curved surface of the Earth, measured in angular units (degrees)
Projected Coordinate System (PCS) — locations on a flat surface, measured in linear units (meters, feet)

In sf, three tools:



Function
Does




st_crs()
Retrieve CRS from an sf or sfc object


st_set_crs()
Set or replace CRS (no coordinate transformation)


st_transform()
Transform coordinates from one CRS to another

title: Week 2
text:
Geographic Coordinate Systems
A GCS identifies locations on the curved surface of the Earth using angular measurements from the center:

Latitude — vertical angle (North/South from equator)
Longitude — horizontal angle (East/West from prime meridian)
North and East are positive; South and West are negative


A GCS is defined by three components:

Ellipsoid — the mathematical model of Earth’s shape (flattened sphere, not perfect)
Datum — how the ellipsoid is anchored to the real Earth (locally fitted or globally centered)
Prime meridian — the origin of longitude (Greenwich, 0°E/W)

Why this matters: two datasets may use the same coordinates but different datums. The difference is small (sub-meter) but compounds in spatial joins and distance calculations.

title: Week 2
text:
Common Datums in Water Resources
Three datums account for most US data:









Datum
Acronym
Used by
Typical error vs. NAD83




North American Datum 1983
NAD83
NHDPlus, most USGS vector data
Reference datum


World Geodetic System 1984
WGS84
GPS, NWIS gauges, web maps
<1 meter in CONUS


NAD27 (historic)
NAD27
Legacy sources only
Can be 100+ meters off









Note


NAD83 and WGS84 differ by less than 1 meter for most of CONUS. But they are not the same CRS. Mixing them without explicit transformation introduces sub-meter errors that compound in spatial joins. Always check with st_crs(a) == st_crs(b) before joining.

title: Week 2
text:
Projected Coordinate Systems
A Projected Coordinate System (PCS) transforms the curved Earth onto a 2D plane. Every transformation introduces distortion.

Three main projection families:












Planar — flat surface touches globe at a point (best for polar regions)
Cylindrical — cylinder wraps around globe (world maps, Mercator)
Conic — cone around globe (mid-latitude areas, CONUS)

title: Week 2
text:
Spatial Properties and Distortion
Each type of projection prioritizes one property at the cost of others:








Property
Preserved by
Used for




Area
Equal-area (Albers)
Accurate area calculations, choropleth maps


Distance
Equidistant
Distance from a fixed center point


Shape
Conformal (Mercator)
Navigation, preserving local angles


Direction
Azimuthal
Navigation from a pole

title: Week 2
text:
Projection Choice: Water Resources Defaults
For CONUS analysis, use these defaults:






Important



Computing area (choropleth maps, watershed statistics) → EPSG:5070 (Albers Equal Area). This is the standard federal projection for CONUS.
Measuring distance (gauge to outlet, confluences, dam spacing) → Keep data in geographic (WGS84, EPSG:4326) and use st_distance() with default S2 spherical geometry — it’s geodesic and correct.
Sub-state local analysis → Use a local UTM zone (e.g., NAD83 / UTM zone 13) if you need projected planar distance.
Visualization/mapping → Use whatever looks right for your region (Web Mercator for web, Albers for print).

title: Week 2
text:
EPSG Codes and PROJ Strings
sf stores CRS in two ways:

EPSG code — integer ID for a known CRS (e.g., 4326 = WGS84 geographic)
PROJ4 string — generic text description understood by the PROJ library

Common codes for water resources work:








EPSG
Name
Use




4326
WGS84 geographic
GPS coordinates, web maps, NWIS gauges


4269
NAD83 geographic
NHDPlus, most USGS vector data


5070
NAD83 / Conus Albers
Area calculations, CONUS-wide analysis


26913–26915
UTM NAD83 zones 13–15
Local/state-level distance calculations



Practical rule: Use EPSG:5070 for CONUS area calculations; use a local UTM (e.g., NAD83 / UTM zones) for sub-state analyses.

title: Week 2
text:
Checking and Setting CRS



st_crs(conus)$epsg
#> [1] 4326
st_crs(conus)$proj4string
#> [1] "+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84 +no_defs"
st_crs(conus)$datum
#> [1] "WGS84"



conus5070 <- st_transform(conus, 5070)
st_crs(conus5070)$epsg
#> [1] 5070
st_crs(conus5070)$proj4string
#> [1] "+proj=aea +lat_0=23 +lon_0=-96 +lat_1=29.5 +lat_2=45.5 +x_0=0 +y_0=0 +datum=NAD83 +units=m +no_defs"

title: Week 2
text: Visualizing Projections

title: Week 2
text:
#1 Reproducibility Habit: Always Check CRS
Before any spatial operation — joins, distance calculations, area calculations — verify CRS match:

# Guard pattern: check before joining
if (st_crs(gauges) != st_crs(flowlines)) {
  flowlines <- st_transform(flowlines, st_crs(gauges))
}

# Or use the equality check
st_crs(gauges) == st_crs(flowlines)  # must be TRUE


Real example: NWIS gauges (WGS84, EPSG:4326) + NHD flowlines (NAD83, EPSG:4269):

st_crs(4326) == st_crs(4269)    # FALSE — they are not the same!
#> [1] FALSE

They look similar (sub-meter differences in CONUS), but snapping a point to a line or computing a distance will be subtly wrong without transformation.






Important


sf will warn you about CRS mismatch but won’t stop you. The result will execute and look plausible — but numbers will be wrong. Build the guard-check habit now.

title: Week 2
text:
Geodesic vs. Planar Measurements
Geodesic distance: shortest path on an ellipsoid — true Earth surface distance.
Planar distance: Euclidean distance in projected coordinates — fast but introduces error.

pts <- data.frame(y = c(40.7128, 34.4208), x = c(-74.0060, -119.6982)) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 4326)

st_distance(pts)                    # Geodesic: ~3,962 km (correct)
st_distance(st_transform(pts, 5070))# Planar: ~3,950 km (distorted)








Important


For water resources: use geodesic (default). In geographic CRS, st_distance() automatically computes geodesic (spherical) distances — correct for continental scales.











Note


sf uses geodesic by default in geographic CRS. Toggle S2 with sf::sf_use_s2(TRUE/FALSE) for fine control (rarely needed).











Note


Performance: S2 geodesic calculations used to be substantially slower, but modern versions of sf and the S2 library have optimized performance significantly. Geodesic is now only ~25% slower than planar for large operations — a measurable but not critical difference for most workflows. Use geodesic unless you’re profiling and find it’s a real bottleneck.

title: Week 2
text:
Units Workflow: Create → Convert → Drop
Create units naturally from measurements, convert between units, then drop before plotting or filtering:
Convert between units with the units package:

co <- AOI::aoi_get(state = "CO")
(l = st_length(st_cast(co, "MULTILINESTRING")))
#> 2100640 [m]

units::set_units(l, "km")
#> 2100.64 [km]
units::set_units(l, "mile")
#> 1305.277 [mile]

(a = st_area(co))
#> 2.69382e+11 [m^2]

units::set_units(a, "ha")
#> 26938196 [ha]
units::set_units(a, "km2")
#> 269382 [km^2]


Strip units when needed for arithmetic or plotting:

units::drop_units(l)
#> [1] 2100640
as.numeric(l)
#> [1] 2100640

title: Week 2
section: Units Are a Class — Know the Rules
text:
Units Are a Class — Know the Rules
Units enforce dimensional correctness but can surprise you:

st_length(conus) + 100   # can't add meters + unitless number

filter(cities, dist_to_border < 160)  # may warn or fail


The corrected patterns:

# Create numeric version for filtering/plotting
cities <- cities |>
  mutate(dist_to_border_km = as.numeric(units::set_units(dist_to_border, "km")))

# Now filter and plot safely
cities |>
  filter(dist_to_border_km < 160) |>
  ggplot(aes(color = dist_to_border_km)) +
  geom_sf()

title: Week 2
text:
Two Essential Data Packages
The lab uses two packages you will reach for constantly in water resources work:


tigris — US Census Bureau TIGER/Line boundaries

library(tigris)
options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)

# State boundaries
states(cb = TRUE, progress_bar = FALSE)

# County boundaries
counties(state = "CO", cb = TRUE, progress_bar = FALSE)

Returns sf objects directly. cb = TRUE gives simplified cartographic boundaries — faster for analysis.

rnaturalearth — country and continent boundaries

library(rnaturalearth)

ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf") |>
  filter(admin %in% c("United States of America",
                      "Canada", "Mexico"))

returnclass = "sf" returns an sf object directly. Filter on the admin column for specific countries.

title: Week 2
text:
Building sf from a CSV
When coordinates are stored as numeric columns in a CSV — the most common format for point data from APIs, sensors, and databases — use st_as_sf():

cities <- read_csv("data/uscities.csv") |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lng", "lat"),  # column names: X first, then Y
           crs    = 4326)             # raw lat/lon is almost always WGS84


Three things to always specify:

coords = — column names in order X (longitude), Y (latitude)
crs = — the CRS the raw numbers are in (not what you want them in)
Then st_transform() to convert to your analysis CRS

title: Week 2
text:
The Spatial File Format Problem
The real world doesn’t use one file format. Water resources agencies publish data in:

Shapefiles (USGS, NOAA — legacy, fragmented)
GeoPackage (modern databases — NHDPlus HR)
GeoJSON (web APIs — USGS, Google)
NetCDF (climate data — NOAA, NCAR)
HDF5 (satellite imagery — Landsat, MODIS)
Proprietary (Esri FileGeodatabase, GeoTIFF variants)


If R’s sf had to write code for every format, it would have thousands of functions and hundreds of library dependencies.
The solution: GDAL — the industry standard library that reads and writes all formats through a unified interface.

title: Week 2
text:
What Is GDAL?
GDAL = Geospatial Data Abstraction Layer
A C++ library (developed by OSGeo, used by every GIS software) that:

Abstracts file formats — speaks shapefile, GeoJSON, GeoPackage, etc., but exposes the same API to your program
Translates between formats — convert any format to any other with one command
Manages drivers — each format has a “driver” (code that knows how to read/write that specific format)
Handles metadata — CRS, bounds, layer names, attribute types



# GDAL (C++ library) <- drivers (one per format)
#     ├── Shapefile driver
#     ├── GeoJSON driver
#     ├── GeoPackage driver
#     ├── GeoTIFF driver
#     ├── NetCDF driver
#     └── ... 200+ more

NOAA climate grids


HDF5
HDF5
.h5
NASA satellite data











Important


GeoPackage replaces Shapefiles: one file, complete metadata, SQLite-based. Shapefiles require sidecars (.shx, .dbf, .prj) and lack metadata. Use GeoPackage when possible.

title: Week 2
text:
Practical Workflow: Checking Drivers
Before downloading a big dataset or writing code to read a file format you haven’t used:

# What drivers do I have?
sf::st_drivers() |> filter(grepl("GeoTIFF|NetCDF|HDF5", name))

# Can GDAL write this format?
sf::st_drivers(type = "vector")[, c("name", "write")]

# What layers are in this file?
st_layers("databases/nhdplus.gpkg")

This prevents silent failures where you think you’re reading a file but GDAL can’t find the driver on your system.

title: Week 2
section: Reading Spatial Files: Shapefiles, GeoJSON, and GeoPackage
text:
Reading Spatial Files: Shapefiles, GeoJSON, and GeoPackage
For pre-built spatial data (boundaries, networks, rasters), use st_read(). The GDAL library (integrated into sf) auto-detects format and reads dozens of file types:

# Shapefile (most common)
states <- st_read("data/tl_2023_us_state/tl_2023_us_state.shp")

# GeoJSON (web-friendly, human-readable)
watersheds <- st_read("data/watersheds.geojson")

# GeoPackage (single-file, database-like, modern standard)
nhdplus <- st_read("databases/nhdplus.gpkg", layer = "flowlines")

# GeoTIFF (raster — not sf, but mentioned for context)
# dem <- terra::rast("elevation/dem.tif")


Common GDAL drivers for water resources:









Format
Extension
When to use
Notes




Shapefile
.shp
Legacy data, USGS sources
Requires 3+ sidecar files (.dbf, .shx, .prj)


GeoJSON
.geojson
Web APIs, GitHub, lightweight sharing
Text-based, human-readable


GeoPackage
.gpkg
Modern standard, large datasets
SQLite-based, single file, efficient


GeoTIFF
.tif
Raster data (DEMs, satellite)
Use terra::rast() not st_read()











Tip


Shapefiles look like one file (.shp) but require 3–4 sidecars (.shx, .dbf, .prj). Zip them together when sharing. GeoPackage is the modern replacement — one file, one st_read() call, no sidecars.

title: Week 2
Week 2
text:
st_filter() — Spatial Subsetting
st_filter() is the spatial equivalent of dplyr::filter() — it keeps only features that satisfy a spatial predicate (default: intersection):

# Keep only cities inside CONUS states
cities_conus <- cities |>
  st_filter(st_union(states))

This is how you clip a point dataset to a polygon boundary — one of the most common operations in spatial data preparation.

title: Week 2
text:
End-to-End: CSV → Filtered → Transformed → Measured
This is the complete workflow to compute the distance from every city to the national border:

# Pre-compute boundary in projected space (outside the pipeline)
boundary <- st_cast(st_union(st_transform(conus, 5070)), "MULTILINESTRING")

# Main workflow: read, build, transform, measure
system.time({
cities <- read_csv("data/uscities.csv", show_col_types =FALSE) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lng", "lat"), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(5070) %>%
  mutate(
    dist_to_border_m = st_distance(., boundary),
    dist_to_border_km = units::set_units(dist_to_border_m, "km")
  )
})
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>   1.665   0.018   1.633

# user  system elapsed 
# 1.648   0.014   1.677

Key takeaways: - Build sf: CSV coordinates + CRS they’re in → st_as_sf() - Transform: project to EPSG:5070 for measurements - Measure: distance returns units object; convert as needed - Reuse: pass pre-computed boundary to st_distance() — clean, fast, readable

title: Week 2
text:
set_units() with Distances
The lab uses set_units() to convert and label distance results:

cities <- cities |>
  mutate(dist_to_border = set_units(st_distance(geometry, us_border), "km"))







Tip


Remember: set_units() returns a units object. Convert to numeric before comparisons or filtering, e.g. filter(cities, as.numeric(dist_to_border) < 160) or create a numeric column with dist_to_border_km <- as.numeric(set_units(dist_to_border, "km")).



st_distance() returns distances in the units of the CRS — meters for projected systems. set_units() converts and labels:

d <- st_distance(st_transform(pts, eqdc))
d                               # meters, labeled [m]
set_units(d, "km")              # km, still labeled
as.numeric(set_units(d, "km"))  # numeric — drop units for plotting/filtering


Always use as.numeric() before comparison operators:

filter(cities, as.numeric(dist_to_border) < 160)  # correct
filter(cities, dist_to_border < 160)               # may warn or fail

title: Week 2
text:
ggrepel: Non-Overlapping Labels
ggrepel solves label collision — essential any time you label points on a map:

library(ggrepel)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = conus, fill = "white") +
  geom_sf(data = st_filter(cities, st_transform(conus, 5070)), color = "red", size = 0.1) +
  ggrepel::geom_label_repel(
    data = filter(cities, city == "Denver"),
    aes(geometry = geometry, label = city),
    stat = "sf_coordinates",  # extracts coordinates from sf geometry
    size = 3
  ) +
  theme_void()


stat = "sf_coordinates" is the key argument — it tells ggrepel to extract X/Y from the geometry column rather than expecting explicit x and y aesthetics. Without it, you get an error.

title: Week 2
text:
gghighlight: Emphasize a Subset
gghighlight greys out features that do not meet a condition, keeping them as spatial context:

library(gghighlight)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = conus) +
  geom_sf(data = st_filter(cities, st_transform(conus, 5070)),
          aes(color = as.numeric(dist_to_border_km)),
          size = 0.3) +
  gghighlight(as.numeric(dist_to_border_km) < 100) +
  scale_color_gradient(low = "orange", high = "darkred") +
  labs(title = "Cities within 100 km of the national border",
       color = "Distance (km)") +
  theme_void()


Features outside the condition are rendered in grey at reduced opacity — they provide spatial context without competing visually with the highlighted subset. Works with any geom_* — points, lines, polygons.

title: Week 2
text:
Everything You’ve Learned Applied
Lab 2 puts all these pieces together on real US cities data:
Your workflow:

Read US cities CSV with lat/lon coordinates
Build sf object with st_as_sf()
Filter to CONUS using st_filter() (spatial subset)
Transform to equal-area CRS (EPSG:5070) for distance calculations
Compute distance from each city to the nearest national border
Identify which cities fall within 160 km of international/state borders
Analyze the result: which states are “border-proximate” and why it matters for federal policy

Skills you’ll use:

Spatial data types and classes (sf, sfc, geometry types)
Coordinate systems and transformations (check CRS, transform to analysis CRS)
Distance measurements (geodesic by default, units handling)
Spatial subsetting (st_filter() as a spatial predicate)
Spatial visualization (geom_sf(), ggrepel, gghighlight)

text:
What We Covered


Simple Features

The ISO standard and its R implementation
The big 7 geometry types
sfg → sfc → sf class hierarchy
WKT / WKB encodings
Casting, combining, dissolving
Sticky geometry + geom_sf()

Coordinate Systems

GCS: ellipsoid, geoid, datum
PCS: projection types and distortion

Always check CRS before joining


Measurements

Geodesic vs. planar distance
st_distance(), st_area(), st_length()
Units as an S3 class — set_units(), drop_units()
Converting and dropping units

Key habits built today:

st_is_valid() on every dataset you read
st_crs(a) == st_crs(b) before every spatial join
Use equal-area CRS for areas, equidistant for distances
as.numeric() before filtering on unit quantities

title: Week 2
section: When you call filter() on a grouped dataframe, R internally does:
text:
When you call filter() on a grouped dataframe, R internally does:

Check: “What class is this object?” (grouped_df)
Look for filter.grouped_df()
If it exists, call it; if not, fall back to filter.data.frame()
The filter.grouped_df() method applies the condition within each group — the key behavior

Compare the same code on grouped vs ungrouped data:

df <- data.frame(site = c("A", "A", "B", "B"), flow = c(100, 120, 95, 110))

# On ungrouped data: keeps rows where flow > 105
df |> filter(flow > 105)
#>   site flow
#> 1    A  120
#> 2    B  110

# On grouped data: keeps earliest row per group where flow > 105
df |> group_by(site) |> filter(flow > 105)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#> # Groups:   site [2]
#>   site   flow
#>   <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 A       120
#> 2 B       110

The function is identical; the method dispatched changes based on class.

title: Week 2
text:
When you call filter() on a grouped dataframe, R internally does:

Check: “What class is this object?” (grouped_df)
Look for filter.grouped_df()
If it exists, call it; if not, fall back to filter.data.frame()
The filter.grouped_df() method applies the condition within each group — the key behavior

Compare the same code on grouped vs ungrouped data:

df <- data.frame(site = c("A", "A", "B", "B"), flow = c(100, 120, 95, 110))

# On ungrouped data: keeps rows where flow > 105
df |> filter(flow > 105)
#>   site flow
#> 1    A  120
#> 2    B  110

# On grouped data: keeps earliest row per group where flow > 105
group_by(df, site) |> filter(flow > 105)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#> # Groups:   site [2]
#>   site   flow
#>   <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 A       120
#> 2 B       110

The function is identical; the method dispatched changes based on class.

title: Week 2
section: Building Geometries: From Points to Polygons
text:
Building Geometries: From Points to Polygons
The big 7 aren’t arbitrary. They compose from simpler to more complex:
Points are the foundation:

pt <- st_point(c(-104.99, 39.74))   # One coordinate: (x, y)


Lines are sequences of connected points:

# 3 points connected by straight segments
line <- st_linestring(rbind(c(-104.99, 39.74),
                             c(-105.10, 39.80),
                             c(-105.15, 39.85)))



Polygons are closed lines that enclose area (first point = last point):

# Same 3 points, but closed: return to start
ring <- rbind(c(-104.99, 39.74), c(-105.10, 39.80), c(-105.15, 39.85), c(-104.99, 39.74))
poly <- st_polygon(list(ring))

Then Multi- variants are just sets of the same type (e.g., MultiPolygon = set of 3 separate polygons). GEOMETRYCOLLECTION is a set of mixed types.

title: Week 2
text:
POINT
A point is composed of one coordinate pair in a specific coordinate system.

Points have no length or area
Example: a gauge location, a dam, a city


ggplot() + 
  geom_point(aes(x = c(1, 2, 3), y = c(3, 1, 2)), size = 3) + 
  labs(x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude") +
  theme_linedraw()

title: Week 2
text:
LINESTRING
A linestring is composed of an ordered sequence of two or more coordinate points.

Points in a line are called vertices and explicitly define the connection between two points
A line has length, but no area
Example: a stream centerline, a river reach, a road


ggplot() + 
  geom_line(aes(x = c(1, 2, 3), y = c(3, 1, 2)), linewidth = 1) + 
  geom_point(aes(x = c(1, 2, 3), y = c(3, 1, 2)), col = "red", size = 3) + 
  labs(x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude") +
  theme_linedraw()

title: Week 2
text:
POLYGON
A polygon is composed of 4 or more points whose starting and ending point are the same.

Polygons enclose a closed ring (first point = last point)
Polygons have both length and area
Example: a watershed boundary, a county border, a floodplain


ggplot() + 
  geom_polygon(aes(x = c(1, 2, 3, 1), y = c(3, 1, 2, 3)), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5, color = "black") + 
  geom_point(aes(x = c(1, 2, 3), y = c(3, 1, 2)), col = "red", size = 3) +
  labs(x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude") +
  theme_linedraw()

title: Week 2
text:
Multi-Geometries and Collections
Multi- variants are just sets of the same type:

MULTIPOINT = set of points
MULTILINESTRING = set of lines (e.g., a braided river system)
MULTIPOLYGON = set of polygons (e.g., an island chain, a fragmented watershed)

GEOMETRYCOLLECTION = a set of mixed geometry types (rare, usually from intersections)

title: Week 2
section: Geometry as a List Column: The Bridge
text:
Geometry as a List Column: The Bridge
WKT and WKB are intermediate—R’s native geometry storage is a list column. Remember nested lists? They’re key to understanding sfc:

# A simple nested list: list containing lists
list(list(c(1, 2)), list(c(3, 4)), list(c(5, 6)))
#> [[1]]
#> [[1]][[1]]
#> [1] 1 2
#> 
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [[2]][[1]]
#> [1] 3 4
#> 
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> [[3]][[1]]
#> [1] 5 6


A geometry list-column (sfc) is exactly this structure — a column where each cell contains a list (a geometry).
This is why sfc is itself a list of lists, and why:

One row = one feature
Each row’s geometry = one complex object (sfg)
Multiple rows’ geometries = the sfc list-column

This structure is what allows sf to be a data.frame — geometry is just another column, treated like any list-column.

title: Week 2
text:
Combining and Dissolving Geometries
Two key operations for working with geometry sets:
st_combine() — joins geometries while preserving interior boundaries:

(co_combined <- st_combine(co$geometry))
#> Geometry set for 1 feature 
#> Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: -109.0602 ymin: 36.99246 xmax: -102.0415 ymax: 41.00342
#> Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84


st_union() — joins geometries and dissolves interior boundaries (merges into one feature):

(co_unioned <- st_union(co$geometry))
#> Geometry set for 1 feature 
#> Geometry type: POLYGON
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: -109.0602 ymin: 36.99246 xmax: -102.0415 ymax: 41.00342
#> Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84

title: Week 2
text:
Visualizing Combine vs. Union


st_combine (boundaries preserved):










st_union (boundaries dissolved):











Water resources example: Use st_combine() to keep sub-basins separate, use st_union() to create a single merged basin outline.

title: Week 2
text:
When you call st_read("data.shp"), here’s what happens:

R/sf calls GDAL: “Read this file”
GDAL looks at the extension (.shp)
GDAL finds the Shapefile driver
The driver reads the .shp and its sidecars
GDAL returns data to sf
sf wraps it in an sfc geometry + sf object structure and hands it to your R code








Note


You don’t write GDAL code directly. But st_read() and st_write() are thin wrappers around GDAL. Understanding this explains why st_read() “just works” on 50+ formats and why format conversions are trivial in R but painful elsewhere.

title: Week 2
section: How Core Libraries Pass Data to R: WKT and WKB
text:
How Core Libraries Pass Data to R: WKT and WKB
When GDAL reads a file or GEOS performs an operation, it uses two standard encodings to pass geometry to R:
Well-Known Text (WKT) — human-readable (you’ll see this in error messages and discussions):

x <- st_linestring(matrix(10:1, 5))
st_as_text(x)
#> [1] "LINESTRING (10 5, 9 4, 8 3, 7 2, 6 1)"


LINESTRING = type; parentheses contain points; points separated by commas; coordinates separated by spaces

Well-Known Binary (WKB) — machine-readable, used internally by GDAL/GEOS for speed and lossless communication:

st_as_binary(x)
#>  [1] 01 02 00 00 00 05 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 24 40 00 00 00 00 00 00 14 40
#> [26] 00 00 00 00 00 00 22 40 00 00 00 00 00 00 10 40 00 00 00 00 00 00 20 40 00
#> [51] 00 00 00 00 00 08 40 00 00 00 00 00 00 1c 40 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 40 00 00
#> [76] 00 00 00 00 18 40 00 00 00 00 00 00 f0 3f








Note


You rarely write WKT/WKB directly, but understanding they exist explains why st_read() “just works”—GDAL converts any format to WKB, sf wraps it as an R object, and the roundtrip is seamless.

title: Week 2
section: Storing Geometry: From Coordinates to Nested Lists
text:
Storing Geometry: From Coordinates to Nested Lists
Remember nested lists from Week 1? They’re the key to understanding how R stores spatial data.
A geometry is just a collection of coordinate pairs:

# A simple list of coordinates (one geometry)
c(x = 1, y = 2)
#> x y 
#> 1 2

# A nested list: many geometries, each is a list of coordinates
list(
  list(c(1, 2)),        # First geometry (one point)
  list(c(3, 4)),        # Second geometry (one point)
  list(c(5, 6))         # Third geometry (one point)
)
#> [[1]]
#> [[1]][[1]]
#> [1] 1 2
#> 
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [[2]][[1]]
#> [1] 3 4
#> 
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> [[3]][[1]]
#> [1] 5 6


This nested structure is how R stores multiple geometries side-by-side. Each row in a data.frame can hold one geometry (which itself is a list of coordinates). When you add a geometry column to a data.frame, you’ve created a geometry column — many rows, each containing its own nested geometry structure.

One row = one feature (with attributes + geometry)
Each row’s geometry = one nested structure of coordinates

Column of geometries = all features’ geometries stacked together

title: Week 2
text:
Invalid Examples


Self-intersecting line:

x1 <- st_linestring(cbind(c(0,1,0,1), 
                          c(0,1,1,0)))
st_is_simple(x1)  # FALSE

Invalid polygon (crossing edges):

x2 <- st_polygon(list(cbind(
  c(0,1,1,1,0,0), 
  c(0,0,1,0.6,1,0))))
st_is_valid(x2)  # FALSE












These operations fail silently unless checked.

title: Week 2
text:
Storing Geometry:
Remember nested lists? They’re the key to understanding how R stores spatial data. A geometry is just a collection of coordinate pairs:

# A simple coordinate set (one geometry)
c(x = 1, y = 2)
#> x y 
#> 1 2

# A nested list: many geometries, each is a list of coordinates
list(
  list(c(1, 2)),        # First geometry (one point)
  list(c(3, 4)),        # Second geometry (one point)
  list(c(5, 6))         # Third geometry (one point)
)
#> [[1]]
#> [[1]][[1]]
#> [1] 1 2
#> 
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [[2]][[1]]
#> [1] 3 4
#> 
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> [[3]][[1]]
#> [1] 5 6


This nested structure is how R stores multiple geometries side-by-side. Each row in a data.frame can hold one geometry (which itself is a list of coordinates). When you add a geometry column to a data.frame, you’ve created a geometry column — many rows, each containing its own nested geometry structure.

One row = one feature (with attributes + geometry)
Each row’s geometry = one nested structure of coordinates

Column of geometries = all features’ geometries stacked together

title: Week 2
text:
Storing Geometry: Nested Lists
Remember nested lists? A geometry is just coordinates:

# One geometry: a pair of coordinates
c(x = 1, y = 2)

# Many geometries: nested list of coordinate pairs
list(list(c(1, 2)), list(c(3, 4)), list(c(5, 6)))


R stores multiple geometries side-by-side this way: Each row in a data.frame holds one geometry (which is a list of coordinates). This creates a geometry column — many rows, each with its own nested geometry.

One row = one feature (with attributes + geometry)
Each row’s geometry = one nested coordinate structure

All rows together = a geometry list-column

title: Week 2
text:
Mixed Geometries and Collections
When features have different geometry types, the type becomes GEOMETRY.
Example: A collection with POINT + LINESTRING:

g <- st_sfc(st_point(c(0, 0)), 
            st_linestring(rbind(c(0, 0), c(1, 1))))


Filter by type with st_is():

st_sf(geometry = g) |>
  filter(st_is(geometry, "LINESTRING"))   # keep only lines
#> Simple feature collection with 1 feature and 0 fields
#> Geometry type: LINESTRING
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: 0 ymin: 0 xmax: 1 ymax: 1
#> CRS:           NA
#>                geometry
#> 1 LINESTRING (0 0, 1 1)



When intersections produce mixed types, use st_collection_extract():

pt   <- st_point(c(1, 0))
ls   <- st_linestring(matrix(c(4, 3, 0, 0), ncol = 2))
poly <- st_polygon(list(matrix(c(5.5, 7, 7, 6, 5.5, 0, 0, -0.5, -0.5, 0), ncol = 2)))
collection <- st_geometrycollection(list(pt, ls, poly))

st_collection_extract(collection, "POLYGON")  # extract only polygons

title: Week 2
section: Combine + Cast: From Boundaries to Lines
text:
Combine + Cast: From Boundaries to Lines
You can combine geometries and then cast them to a different type — useful for creating line networks from polygon boundaries:

co_borders_combined <- st_combine(co$geometry) |> st_cast("MULTILINESTRING")
co_borders_unioned  <- st_union(co$geometry) |> st_cast("MULTILINESTRING")









Tip


This distinction matters constantly in water resources: county boundaries vs. watershed boundaries, stream reaches vs. the river network, individual gauge catchments vs. the basin outline.

title: Week 2
text:
What Is S2?
S2 is Google’s spherical geometry library — a modern C++ implementation for accurate calculations on a sphere/ellipsoid.
sf uses S2 under the hood when data is in geographic coordinates (e.g., WGS84). Instead of flattening Earth to a 2D plane (which introduces distortion), S2 works directly with spherical coordinates:

Ellipsoidal geometry — computes distances, intersections, areas on the actual Earth shape
Efficient spatial indexing — divides the sphere into hierarchical cells for fast operations
Replaces GEOS for geographic data — when your CRS is in degrees, S2 handles the heavy lifting
Fast enough in practice — modern optimizations have made geodesic calculations competitive with planar








Important


S2 is automatic: if your data is in geographic coordinates, st_distance(), st_intersects(), and other spatial operations use S2 geodesic calculations by default. You don’t need to do anything.

title: Week 2
text:
Controlling S2: When and How
S2 is the right default for water resources work (continental scales, mixed coordinate systems), but you can toggle it for specialized cases:

# Disable S2 (use GEOS planar geometry instead)
sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)

# Re-enable S2
sf::sf_use_s2(TRUE)

# Check current setting
sf::sf_use_s2()


When to disable S2: - Very small local areas (< 10 km) where planar error is negligible and you want marginal speed gains - Specialized geometric algorithms that require GEOS planar operations (rare in practice)
Leave S2 enabled (default): - Continental and larger scales (your typical water resources workflow) - Mixing geographic and projected data - When correctness matters more than squeezing out microseconds

title: Week 2
text:
Common Pitfalls ⚠️
Pitfall: Distances in Geographic Space

boundary <- st_cast(st_union(conus),"MULTILINESTRING")

cities <- read_csv("data/uscities.csv") |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lng", "lat"), crs = 4326) %>%
  mutate(dist = st_distance(., boundary))

# user    system  elapsed
# 80.763  0.300   81.055

Rule: Transform geometry to projected CRS before expensive operations like st_union(), st_intersection(), etc.

title: Week 2
text:
geom_sf(): The Foundation
geom_sf() is ggplot2’s spatial geometry layer. It automatically extracts coordinates from the geometry column and plots them. No need to specify x and y aesthetics.


Points

ggplot(cities) +
  geom_sf(color = "navy", size = 1)


Polygons

ggplot(conus) +
  geom_sf(fill = "lightblue", color = "black")



Key advantage: All standard ggplot2 aesthetics work — color, fill, size, alpha, linetype, etc. And you can layer multiple geom_sf() calls:

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = conus, fill = "white") +
  geom_sf(data = st_filter(cities, st_transform(conus, 5070)), color = "red", size = 0.1) +
  theme_void()







Tip


Always add theme_void() to remove axes, gridlines, and background — maps don’t need Cartesian coordinates.

title: Week 2
text:
Next Week

title: Week 3, Part 1
text:
Last Week: Measurements and Coordinates
You learned how to:

Measure spatial data: distances, areas, lengths (GEOS library)
Transform between coordinate systems (PROJ library)
Distinguish between geodesic (curved Earth) and planar (flat space) calculations
Understand how S2 geometry makes geodesic calculations practical


Key insight: Spatial libraries (GDAL, PROJ, GEOS, S2) handle the math. Your job: ask the right questions and interpret the results correctly.

title: Week 3, Part 1
text:
Geometry Has Structure
Every geometry has three parts:

Interior — the space inside the geometry (0D, 1D, or 2D depending on type)
Boundary — the edge or envelope that defines the limit
Exterior — everything outside


This structure matters for answering questions like:

Does this polygon contain that point?
Does this stream intersect that watershed?
Are these county boundaries touching with no overlap?

title: Week 3, Part 1
text:
Interior, Boundary, Exterior: Examples


POINT (0D) - Interior: the point itself - Boundary: empty - Exterior: everything else

LINESTRING (1D) - Interior: all points except endpoints - Boundary: the two endpoints - Exterior: everything else

POLYGON (2D) - Interior: the area enclosed - Boundary: the rings (edges) - Exterior: outside the rings

title: Week 3, Part 1
text:
Asking “What’s the relationship?”
When two geometries meet or overlap, we can ask: exactly what kind of relationship exists?
This is formalized in the Dimensionally Extended 9-Intersection Model (DE-9IM), a mathematical framework that tests all possible intersections between two geometries.
Key insight: The type of overlap tells you the spatial relationship.

Point AND point overlapping = intersection
Line AND boundary = touching (but not overlapping internally)
Area AND area with gap at edge = overlapping

title: Week 3, Part 1
text:
The Matrix in Practice
For practical purposes, we simplify to True/False (non-empty = T):

Intersects — geometries share any space
Touches — boundaries meet, but interiors don’t overlap
Within — geometry A is completely inside geometry B
Contains — geometry A completely encloses geometry B
Crosses — geometries overlap in a lower dimension (line crosses polygon)
Overlaps — same dimension, partial overlap








Important


These predicates are topological — they depend only on spatial relationships, not on coordinates or CRS. A result stays true even if you transform the CRS.

title: Week 3
text:
Named predicates in R

sf provides a set of functions that implement the DE-9IM model and named predicates. Each of these can return either a sparse or dense matrix.

sparse matrix

#> Sparse geometry binary predicate list of length 3, where the predicate
#> was `intersects'
#>  1: 1, 3
#>  2: 2, 3
#>  3: 3

dense matrix

#>       [,1]  [,2] [,3]  [,4]
#> [1,]  TRUE FALSE TRUE FALSE
#> [2,] FALSE  TRUE TRUE FALSE
#> [3,] FALSE FALSE TRUE FALSE
#>       [,1]  [,2]  [,3] [,4]
#> [1,] FALSE  TRUE FALSE TRUE
#> [2,]  TRUE FALSE FALSE TRUE
#> [3,]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE TRUE
#>       [,1]  [,2]  [,3]  [,4]
#> [1,] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE
#> [2,] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE
#> [3,] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE
#>       [,1]  [,2]  [,3]  [,4]
#> [1,] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE
#> [2,] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE
#> [3,] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE

title: Week 3, Part 1
text:
Dense vs. Sparse Results
For human readability, use sparse = FALSE:

st_intersects(states, wa, sparse = FALSE)
#      [,1]
# [1,] FALSE  # Oregon
# [2,] FALSE  
# [3,]  TRUE  # Montana touches Washington
# [4,]  TRUE  # Idaho touches Washington

This gives you a logical matrix for filtering.

title: Week 3, Part 1
section: The Power of Predicates: Filter by Space
text:
The Power of Predicates: Filter by Space
Instead of filtering by a column value (name == "Washington"), filter by a spatial relationship:

# Traditional filter (attribute-based)
filter(states, name == "Washington")

# Spatial filter (predicate-based)
st_filter(states, wa, .predicate = st_touches)

Both return subsets of states, but spatial filter uses topology.

Default predicate is st_intersects — returns all geometries that touch or overlap the target.

st_filter(states, wa)  # = st_filter(states, wa, .predicate = st_intersects)

title: Week 3, Part 1
section: Real Example: Which States Touch Washington?
text:
Real Example: Which States Touch Washington?

wa_neighbors <- st_filter(states, wa, .predicate = st_touches)

title: Week 3, Part 1
text:
Distance-Based Filtering
Predicates can also use distance thresholds:

# "Which cities are within 100 km of Fort Collins?"
fc <- filter(cities, city == "Fort Collins")

nearby_cities <- st_filter(
  cities, 
  fc, 
  .predicate = st_is_within_distance, 
  dist = 100000  # units in CRS (meters for geographic)
)

Distance units match the CRS: - Geographic CRS (WGS84): meters - Projected CRS (EPSG:5070): meters - Must account for CRS when specifying distance

Hydrology applications: - Which stream gauges are within 50 km upstream? - Which reservoirs are within 100 km of this city? - Which monitoring stations bracket this watershed outlet?

title: Week 3, Part 1
text:
From Filtering to Joining
Filtering: Subset one dataset based on spatial relationship to another (select rows).
Joining: Combine columns from two datasets based on spatial relationships (connect datasets).

Filter → Returns subset of x
Join → Returns all of x with columns from matching y rows appended

Joins are where spatial analysis becomes truly powerful — merging data from multiple sources using space as the key.

title: Week 3, Part 1
text:
st_join: Add Spatial Context

# For each city, which state is it in?
cities_with_state <- st_join(cities, states)

Returns cities with all columns from states added where the spatial predicate is true.

Types of joins:

Left join (default): Keep all rows from cities, add matching state data
Inner join: Keep only cities that match (filter-like behavior)

title: Week 3, Part 1
section: Example: Which County Has the Most Starbucks?

title: Week 3, Part 1
section: Water Resources Example: Points in Polygons
text:
Water Resources Example: Points in Polygons

# Which stream gauges fall within each watershed?
gauges_in_watershed <- st_join(gauges, watersheds)

# Summarize: average discharge per watershed
discharge_by_watershed <- gauges_in_watershed |>
  group_by(watershed_id) |>
  summarise(mean_discharge = mean(discharge_m3s))

This pattern is ubiquitous in spatial analysis.

title: Week 3, Part 1
text:
This Week: Topology & Relationships
You now know:

Spatial predicates (intersects, touches, within, etc.) test topological relationships
Spatial filtering (st_filter) subsets data by these relationships
Spatial joining (st_join) adds columns based on relationships


Next week: Simplification (reduce geometry complexity) and tessellation (divide space into tiles).

title: Week 3, Part 1
text:
The DE-9IM Matrix Structure
For geometries a and b, test 9 intersections:
\[\begin{bmatrix} I_a \cap I_b & I_a \cap B_b & I_a \cap E_b \\ B_a \cap I_b & B_a \cap B_b & B_a \cap E_b \\ E_a \cap I_b & E_a \cap B_b & E_a \cap E_b \end{bmatrix}\]
Where: - I = interior (the “inside”) - B = boundary (the edge) - E = exterior (everything outside)
Each cell records what dimension of overlap occurs: - F = False (empty, no intersection) - 0 = Point (0D intersection) - 1 = Line (1D intersection) - 2 = Area (2D intersection) - * = Any dimension (wildcard in some systems)
