title: Lab 3: Answer Key
section: Step 7.2 — Compute spatial lags and attribute correlation
text:
Step 7.2 — Compute spatial lags and attribute correlation

# Use the same row-standardized neighbor weights from Q6
neighbor_weights <- neighbor_weights_hex

# Extract attributes (vectors)
year_complete <- hexagon_attrs$mean_year
area_acres <- hexagon_attrs$mean_area
dam_count <- hexagon_attrs$n_dams

# Impute NAs (tiles with no dams) using global mean for year/area
year_complete_impute <- ifelse(is.na(year_complete), mean(year_complete, na.rm = TRUE), year_complete)
area_acres_impute <- ifelse(is.na(area_acres), mean(area_acres, na.rm = TRUE), area_acres)

# Compute spatial lag: W * x (average attribute value in neighbors)
year_lag <- as.vector(neighbor_weights %*% year_complete_impute)
area_lag <- as.vector(neighbor_weights %*% area_acres_impute)
count_lag <- as.vector(neighbor_weights %*% dam_count)

# Correlation: original value vs. its spatial lag
# Only correlate where original data exists (don't use imputed values for correlation)
valid_year <- !is.na(year_complete)
valid_area <- !is.na(area_acres)

cor_year <- cor(year_complete[valid_year], year_lag[valid_year], use = "complete.obs")
cor_area <- cor(area_acres[valid_area], area_lag[valid_area], use = "complete.obs")
cor_count <- cor(dam_count, count_lag, use = "complete.obs")

spatial_dependence <- data.frame(
  Attribute = c("Mean Year Completed", "Mean Surface Area", "Dam Count"),
  Correlation_with_Spatial_Lag = c(cor_year, cor_area, cor_count),
  Strength = c(
    ifelse(abs(cor_year) > 0.5, "Strong", ifelse(abs(cor_year) > 0.2, "Moderate", "Weak")),
    ifelse(abs(cor_area) > 0.5, "Strong", ifelse(abs(cor_area) > 0.2, "Moderate", "Weak")),
    ifelse(abs(cor_count) > 0.5, "Strong", ifelse(abs(cor_count) > 0.2, "Moderate", "Weak"))
  )
)

title: Lab 3: Answer Key
section: Step 7.4 — Interpretation and spatial regression implication
text:
Step 7.4 — Interpretation and spatial regression implication
a. Which dam attributes show strong spatial clustering?
Dam count shows the strongest spatial structure (correlation with lag = 0.701), confirming Moran’s I = 0.385 from Q6. Year completed (r = 0.623) also clusters: historic construction booms (1950s TVA) and modern buildouts (1990s Southwest) are regional phenomena, not scattered. Surface area shows lighter clustering (r = 0.521), suggesting dam size is determined partly by local geology/hydrology rather than purely regional infrastructure decisions.
Why this matters: Historic dams (Tennessee, Arkansas, Oklahoma) cluster because they reflect federal policy (TVA era), not random placement. Modern dams (Texas, California) cluster because of regional demand and suitable geography. These clustered temporal patterns suggest hidden institutional and environmental variables—factors that drive clustering and should appear in spatial regression models.
b. Outliers and anomalies in the Moran scatterplot
The High-Low (HL) quadrant contains Pacific Northwest and Colorado dams: these are high-count tiles surrounded by neighbors with fewer dams. This occurs because dams concentrate in specific river basins (e.g., Columbia, Colorado) that neighbor lower-dam regions. These outliers are not “anomalies” but spatially structured boundaries—transitions between hydrologic basins. A spatial regression model would flag these as significant while OLS would mis-attribute variance to unmeasured variables.
Low-High (LH) quadrant is rare, suggesting dam distribution favors clustering over dispersion. If LH tiles existed (sparse surrounded by dense), they might represent policy “dams we avoided here but built upstream”—worth investigating with dam purpose and reservoir design data.
c. Why spatial regression is essential
If we regressed “storage capacity ~ year completed” with standard OLS, we’d violate the independence assumption: tiles with similar completion years are neighbors, creating positively autocorrelated residuals. This biases: - Standard errors downward (spuriously narrow confidence intervals) - Hypothesis tests inflated (Type I error rates exceed stated α) - Coefficients unbiased but inefficient (larger variance than spatial models)
A Spatial Autoregressive (SAR) model would instead specify: \[y_i = \rho W y_i + X \beta + \epsilon\]
where \(W y\) (spatial lag of the outcome) captures the fact that storage capacity in neighboring tiles influences your tile’s capacity through hydrologic/management interconnections. This yields valid inference.
Thus: Because neighboring tiles have correlated dam attributes (r = 0.5–0.7), a spatial regression model is strongly recommended for predictive or causal analysis. The hexagon tessellation provides well-defined, uniform neighborhood structures—ideal for SAR estimation.

section: How These Concepts Drive Spatial Stats
text:
How These Concepts Drive Spatial Stats
Spatial predicates enable definition of spatial relationships: - Which observations are neighbors? (st_touches, st_intersects) - What is the distance relationship? (st_is_within_distance, st_buffer) - These relationships form the basis of spatial autocorrelation and dependence structures

Tessellations and aggregation units define the scale of analysis: - Choice of neighborhoods (hexagons vs grids vs Voronoi) affects statistical inference - MAUP means our choice of regions directly influences correlation estimates, regression coefficients, and hypothesis test results - Spatial statistics must account for this uncertainty


Simplification and computational efficiency enable model feasibility: - Spatial statistical models (kriging, spatial regression, CAR models) scale with the number of spatial units - Reducing geometric complexity via simplification can make computationally-intensive models tractable - Trade-off: retain enough detail for meaningful inference

title: Week 3
section: Tessellation Choice Affects Neighbor Structure (and Statistics)
text:
Tessellation Choice Affects Neighbor Structure (and Statistics)
Different tessellations change neighbor structure and therefore statistical estimates (MAUP).
Critical insight: Same point data, different tessellations, different statistical results

title: Week 3
text:
Moran’s I: Detecting Spatial Clustering
Conceptual understanding (formal math comes later):

Moran’s I measures: “Do neighbors have similar values?”


Interpretation:

I > 0 & p < 0.05: 🟢 POSITIVE AUTOCORRELATION

Neighbors have similar values → Genuine clustering
Example: Starbucks stores cluster on coasts (California, New York high; Mountain West low)





I ≈ 0 or p > 0.05: 🟡 NO SIGNIFICANT CLUSTERING

Distribution is random given your neighbor network definition
Observations spread uniformly





I < 0 & p < 0.05: 🔴 NEGATIVE AUTOCORRELATION (rare)

Neighbors have dissimilar values → Regular/dispersed pattern
Example: Coffee shops in a city might spread out (competition for local market)




KEY CONSTRAINT: Moran’s I depends critically on your spatial weights matrix W - Different tessellations → Different W → Different I → Different conclusions - Choose tessellation based on domain knowledge, not just statistics

title: Week 3
text:
Why Row-Standardize Neighbor Weights?
Without standardization:

#> Region A (4 neighbors): weights = [1, 1, 1, 1] (sum = 4)
#> Region B (8 neighbors): weights = [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] (sum = 8)
#> 
#> Problem: Region B's neighbors have MORE influence (8x total weight vs. 4x)
#> Result: Moran's I inflated in high-connectivity areas ❌


With row-standardization (divide each row by its sum):

#> Region A: weights = [0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25] (sum = 1)
#> Region B: weights = [0.125, 0.125, ..., 0.125] (sum = 1)
#> 
#> Benefit: Each neighbor contributes equally to that region's spatial lag
#> Result: Fair comparison across space ✓
#>         Moran's I has standard interpretation ✓



Practical consequence: Without standardization, isolated regions with few neighbors would underestimate spatial dependence compared to well-connected regions

title: Week 3
section: Spatial Lag: The Foundation of Spatial Statistics
text:
Spatial Lag: The Foundation of Spatial Statistics
Definition:
Spatial lag of variable X at location i = Weighted average of X in neighbors of i

Mathematically:
\[\text{lag}_i = \sum_j w_{ij} \cdot x_j\]
where \(w_{ij}\) is row-standardized weight and j indexes neighbors


In code:

spatial_lag <- W %*% x
# Result: vector where each element is 
# weighted average of neighbors' x values



Why it matters:
If \(\text{correlation}(x, \text{spatial\_lag}(x)) > 0.5\), then: - Neighbors have similar values - Observations are not independent - Standard regression (OLS) breaks down - Need spatial regression models (SAR, SEM, CAR)

title: Week 3
section: Standard Regression Fails with Spatial Data
text:
Standard Regression Fails with Spatial Data
OLS Assumption: Observations are independent (residuals are uncorrelated)

Spatial Data Reality: Nearby regions often have correlated attributes

Starbucks density clusters (coastal cities have high density)
Similar urban development patterns
Regional consumer preferences & market saturation
→ Residuals are correlated, not independent



Consequences of violating independence:



Problem
Impact




Standard errors too narrow
Over-confident estimates


t-statistics inflated
Too many false positives


95% CI doesn’t cover 95%
Invalid inference


Type I error rate > 5%
Wrong conclusions





Solution: Use spatial statistics that explicitly model dependence

Testing: Moran’s I (test for spatial clustering)
Modeling: Spatial Autoregressive (SAR) or Spatial Error (SEM) models
Interpretation: Spatial lag models, Conditional AutoRegressive (CAR) models

title: Week 3
section: LISA: Which Neighborhoods are Clusters vs. Outliers?
text:
LISA: Which Neighborhoods are Clusters vs. Outliers?
Global Moran’s I = Average clustering across entire region
LISA (Local Indicator of Spatial Association) = Clustering at each location

LISA Quadrants (from Moran scatterplot):


🔴 High-High (red)

High value + high neighbors
Cluster of high values
Example: California coast (high Starbucks, neighbors are high)

🔵 Low-Low (blue)

Low value + low neighbors
Cluster of low values
Example: Rural interior states (low Starbucks, neighbors are low)


🟠 High-Low (orange)

High value + low neighbors
Isolated hotspot (outlier)
Example: Denver metro (high Starbucks surrounded by sparse rural states)

🟢 Low-High (green)

Low value + high neighbors
Rare anomaly
Example: Small town on coast (low local Starbucks but high neighbors)

title: Week 3
text:
Spatial statistics needs functions
Example: Computing Moran’s I across different tessellations
You learned this week that spatial statistics depend on neighbor structure:


Without functions:

# Hexagon Moran's I
W_hex <- st_touches(hex_grid)
diag(W_hex) <- 0
W_hex <- W_hex / rowSums(W_hex)
I_hex <- ape::Moran.I(data, W_hex)

# Square Moran's I
W_sq <- st_touches(sq_grid)
diag(W_sq) <- 0
W_sq <- W_sq / rowSums(W_sq)
I_sq <- ape::Moran.I(data, W_sq)

# Voronoi Moran's I
W_vor <- st_touches(vor_grid)
diag(W_vor) <- 0
W_vor <- W_vor / rowSums(W_vor)
I_vor <- ape::Moran.I(data, W_vor)

⚠️ Repetitive, error-prone!

With functions:

compute_morans_i <- function(
    tessellation, 
    data_values) {
  
  # Build neighbor matrix
  W <- st_touches(tessellation, 
                   sparse = FALSE)
  diag(W) <- 0
  W <- W / rowSums(W)
  
  # Compute Moran's I
  ape::Moran.I(data_values, W)
}

# Apply to all tessellations
I_hex <- compute_morans_i(
  hex_grid, data_values)
I_sq <- compute_morans_i(
  sq_grid, data_values)
I_vor <- compute_morans_i(
  vor_grid, data_values)

✅ Consistent, maintainable!


Key insight: The spatial statistics pipeline you learned is now encapsulated in a single reusable function

title: Lab 3: Answer Key
text:
Step 6.4 (Extension) — Distance-Based Neighborhood Sensitivity Analysis
What happens to Moran’s I at different spatial scales?
The touching-predicate captures immediate neighbors. But dam clustering might be strongest at regional scales (100+ km away). This extension tests whether clustering is local or regional.

# Compute distance matrix between hexagon tile centroids (in meters, convert to km)
hex_centroids <- st_centroid(pip_hexagon)
distance_matrix <- st_distance(hex_centroids) / 1000  # Convert to km

# Function to create distance-based neighbor weights
create_distance_neighbors <- function(dist_km, threshold) {
  neighbor_mat <- (dist_km <= units::set_units(threshold, "km")) * 1
  diag(neighbor_mat) <- 0
  
  # Row-standardize
  w <- neighbor_mat / rowSums(neighbor_mat)
  w[!is.finite(w)] <- 0
  return(w)
}

# Create weights for three distance thresholds
w_25km <- create_distance_neighbors(distance_matrix, 25)
w_50km <- create_distance_neighbors(distance_matrix, 50)
w_100km <- create_distance_neighbors(distance_matrix, 100)

# Compute Moran's I for each distance threshold
dam_counts <- pip_hexagon %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% pull(n)

morans_25 <- ape::Moran.I(x = dam_counts, weight = w_25km)
morans_50 <- ape::Moran.I(x = dam_counts, weight = w_50km)
morans_100 <- ape::Moran.I(x = dam_counts, weight = w_100km)

# Summary table
distance_sensitivity <- data.frame(
  Distance_Threshold_km = c(25, 50, 100),
  Morans_I = c(morans_25$observed, morans_50$observed, morans_100$observed),
  P_Value = c(morans_25$p.value, morans_50$p.value, morans_100$p.value),
  Avg_Neighbors = c(
    round(mean(rowSums(w_25km > 0)), 1),
    round(mean(rowSums(w_50km > 0)), 1),
    round(mean(rowSums(w_100km > 0)), 1)
  ),
  Significant = c(
    ifelse(morans_25$p.value < 0.05, "Yes***", "No"),
    ifelse(morans_50$p.value < 0.05, "Yes***", "No"),
    ifelse(morans_100$p.value < 0.05, "Yes***", "No")
  )
)

      digits = 4,

  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE) %>%

Interpretation:
The distance-based analysis reveals clustering robustness across scales. Whether using immediate (25 km) or regional (100 km) neighborhoods, Moran’s I remains around 0.35–0.37. This indicates dam clustering is not a local artifact but a national signal: the South’s dam concentration and Mountain West’s sparseness persist from local to regional scales, suggesting coherent water management strategy across the USA. If clustering were purely local (e.g., individual reservoirs clustered with neighbors), I would decay sharply as distance increased.

title: Week 3
section: From Neighbors to Inference: Why We Need Spatial Statistics
text:
From Neighbors to Inference: Why We Need Spatial Statistics
The central question: Do neighboring observations have similar values?
If YES: - Standard regression breaks (independence assumption violated) - We need spatial statistics to test for clustering and model dependence - The spatial weights matrix W captures neighbor relationships

Why W matters: - Built from geometric relationships: st_touches(), st_intersects(), st_is_within_distance() - Scale depends on tessellation choice (hexagon vs square vs Voronoi) → MAUP - Directly inputs to: Moran’s I, spatial regression (SAR/SEM), LISA, kriging


Section Arc:

Build the neighbor matrix W from geometry (predicates & tessellations)
Test for global clustering with Moran’s I
Visualize local patterns with LISA and spatial-lag plots
Diagnose how spatial dependence breaks OLS and motivates spatial regression

title: Week 3
section: Moran’s I: Does Your Variable Cluster?
text:
Moran’s I: Does Your Variable Cluster?
The question: If two hexagons are neighbors, do they have similar Starbucks counts?
Moran’s I is the answer—a test for spatial autocorrelation

Formula (don’t memorize, conceptually: “weighted correlation of X with its spatial lag”):
\[I = \frac{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}(x_i - \bar{x})(x_j - \bar{x})}{σ^2 \sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}}\]


Interpretation:








I value
Meaning
Starbucks




I > 0, p < 0.05
🟢 Positive clustering
CA hexagons HIGH-HIGH, MT LOW-LOW


I ≈ 0, p > 0.05
🟡 No clustering
Uniform distribution


I < 0, p < 0.05
🔴 Regular pattern
High surrounded by low (rare)





Our result: I = 0.253, p < 0.001 ✓ Significant positive clustering
What this means: Starbucks are geographically concentrated. Coastal and urban hexagons cluster together; rural hexagons cluster together. This is not a random distribution.

title: Week 3
section: Spatial Lag: From Neighbors to Dependence
text:
Spatial Lag: From Neighbors to Dependence
Definition: Spatial lag of X at location i = Weighted average of X in neighbors of i
\[\text{lag}_i = \sum_j w_{ij} \cdot x_j\]

Concrete example (hexagon grid, Starbucks):

# If hexagon #42 has 6 neighbors with counts: [2, 8, 5, 12, 3, 7]
# And each row-standardized weight = 1/6
# Then lag_42 = (1/6)*(2 + 8 + 5 + 12 + 3 + 7) = 6.17 stores in neighbors

# In matrix form:
spatial_lag <- W %*% counts  # One line computes for all hexagons



The critical insight:
If \(\text{correlation}(x, \text{lag}(x)) > 0.5\): - Neighbors have similar values → Strong spatial dependence - Moran’s I will be positive and significant - OLS residuals will be correlated → Standard errors wrong - Solution: SAR, SEM, or CAR models

title: Week 3
text:
The Road Ahead: Spatial Regression
Now that you understand spatial dependence, the next step is modeling it

Three spatial regression approaches:

Spatial Autoregressive (SAR):

\(y = \rho W y + X\beta + \epsilon\)
Neighboring values directly influence your value
Best for: Regional spillover effects





Spatial Error (SEM):

\(\epsilon = \lambda W \epsilon + u\)
Omitted variables create correlated errors

Best for: Unobserved heterogeneity





Conditional AutoRegressive (CAR):

Bayesian approach; specific conditional structure
Best for: Spatial smoothing, hierarchical models





You can now look at any spatial dataset and ask: “Are these observations spatially dependent? Which tessellation makes sense? What does that imply for my statistical model?”
You’ll implement these models in Lab-03.

title: Week 3
section: Deep Dive: Moran’s I & Tests (10 min)
text:
Deep Dive: Moran’s I & Tests (10 min)
Time: ~10 minutes — build intuition, show formula, and test logic
Formula (expanded):
\[I = \frac{n}{S_0} \frac{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}(x_i - \bar{x})(x_j - \bar{x})}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2}\]
where \(S_0 = \sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}\) and \(n\) is the number of units.
Interpretation checklist: - Compare observed I to expected I under spatial randomness (approx. \(-1/(n-1)\)) - Check sign and p-value — positive = clustering, negative = dispersion
Permutation (randomization) test (concept): - Null: values are randomly distributed among locations (keep W fixed) - Procedure: randomly permute x many times (e.g., 999), compute I for each permutation, compare observed I to permutation distribution to get p-value

# Conceptual permutation test (slow to run in slides)
obs <- ape::Moran.I(x, W)$observed
perms <- replicate(999, ape::Moran.I(sample(x), W)$observed)
p_value <- (sum(abs(perms) >= abs(obs)) + 1) / (length(perms) + 1)

Note: production code typically uses spdep::moran.test() or spdep::moran.mc() for permutation tests once listw objects are constructed.

title: Week 3
text:
Geary’s C: complementary measure (3 min)
Time: ~3 minutes — contrast with Moran’s I
Formula:
\[C = \frac{(n-1)}{2S_0} \frac{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}(x_i - x_j)^2}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2}\]

Geary’s C emphasizes local differences (uses squared differences between neighbors)
Interpretation: C < 1 indicates positive spatial autocorrelation (similar neighbors), C > 1 indicates negative autocorrelation; C ≈ 1 under randomness


# Example: geary using spdep (concept)
# listw <- spdep::mat2listw(W)
# spdep::geary.test(x, listw)

title: Week 3
text:
Distance-based neighbors & sensitivity (5–7 min)
Time: ~5–7 minutes — show how neighborhood definition affects I
Why: Different distance thresholds produce different neighbor matrices and therefore different Moran’s I values (scale sensitivity).

# Build distance neighbors (threshold in meters/km)
dist_mat <- st_distance(st_centroid(hex_grid))
thresh <- units::set_units(50000, "m") # 50 km
W_dist <- (dist_mat <= thresh) * 1; diag(W_dist) <- 0
W_dist <- W_dist / rowSums(W_dist); W_dist[!is.finite(W_dist)] <- 0
ape::Moran.I(as.numeric(hex_sb), W_dist)

section: Kriging mini-lecture (10 min) — variogram + ordinary kriging
text:
Kriging mini-lecture (10 min) — variogram + ordinary kriging
Time: ~10 minutes — show empirical variogram, fit a model, and run ordinary kriging
Empirical variogram: measures how similarity decays with distance. We’ll use hexagon counts (centroids) as the observation locations.

# Kriging demo (keeps runtime moderate)
library(gstat)
library(sf)

# prepare centroids with counts (hex_grid and hex_sb expected from earlier chunks)
hex_cent <- st_centroid(hex_grid)
hex_cent$count <- as.numeric(hex_sb)

# project to metric CRS if needed for distance calculations
if (st_is_longlat(hex_cent)) {
  hex_cent <- st_transform(hex_cent, 3857)
}

# convert to Spatial (gstat expects sp objects reliably)
hex_sp <- as(hex_cent, "Spatial")

# empirical variogram
v_emp <- gstat::variogram(count ~ 1, data = hex_sp, cutoff = 500000, width = 50000)

# fit a simple exponential model (start values automatic but we seed sensible defaults)
v_fit <- tryCatch(
  gstat::fit.variogram(v_emp, gstat::vgm(psill = var(hex_cent$count, na.rm=TRUE), model = "Exp", range = 100000, nugget = 0)),
  error = function(e) gstat::vgm(model = "Exp")
)

# prediction grid (coarse, keeps render time small)
pred_points <- st_make_grid(st_union(st_geometry(hex_grid)), cellsize = 50000, what = "centers")
pred_sf <- st_sf(geometry = pred_points)
pred_sf <- st_set_crs(pred_sf, st_crs(hex_cent))
pred_sp <- as(pred_sf, "Spatial")

# ordinary kriging (fast-ish because grid is coarse)
kr <- tryCatch(
  gstat::krige(count ~ 1, hex_sp, pred_sp, model = v_fit),
  error = function(e) {
    # fallback: return NA predictions if kriging fails
    warning("Kriging failed: returning NA grid")
    pred_dummy <- pred_sp
    pred_dummy$var1.pred <- NA
    pred_dummy
  }
)
#> [using ordinary kriging]

# convert to sf for plotting
kr_sf <- st_as_sf(kr)
kr_sf <- st_transform(kr_sf, st_crs(hex_grid))

kr_sf$var1.pred <- as.numeric(kr_sf$var1.pred)

title: Week 3
text:
Deep Dive: Moran’s I & Tests
Formula (expanded):
\[I = \frac{n}{S_0} \frac{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}(x_i - \bar{x})(x_j - \bar{x})}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2}\]
where \(S_0 = \sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}\) and \(n\) is the number of units.
Interpretation checklist

Compare to expectation: observed I vs expected I under spatial randomness (approx. \(-1/(n-1)\)).
Sign & significance: I > 0 indicates clustering, I < 0 indicates dispersion; check p-value for evidence against randomness.
Permutation test: run permutations (e.g., 199–999+) to build a reference distribution for I and obtain a robust p-value.
Check W sensitivity: repeat with alternative neighbor definitions (adjacency, distance, k‑NN) to ensure conclusions are not driven by W.

title: Week 3
text:
Geary’s C: complementary measure
Visual: scatter of neighbor differences vs distance, and a small summary statistic.
Formula:
\[C = \frac{(n-1)}{2S_0} \frac{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}(x_i - x_j)^2}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2}\]

Geary’s C emphasizes local differences (uses squared differences between neighbors)
Interpretation: C < 1 indicates positive spatial autocorrelation (similar neighbors), C > 1 indicates negative autocorrelation; C ≈ 1 under randomness

Interpretation: Geary’s C ≈ NA. Values below 1 indicate similarity between neighbors (positive autocorrelation); the histogram shows the distribution of neighbor squared-differences that underlies this summary.

title: Week 3
text:
Distance-based neighbors & sensitivity
Visual illustration: how Moran’s I changes with distance threshold (illustrative slide).
What the diagnostic does

Plots estimated Moran’s I on the y-axis against the neighborhood threshold (km) on the x-axis.
Each point represents the observed I computed using neighbors defined by the given distance threshold; points are labeled by threshold and in the original plot were colored by whether a small permutation test returned p < 0.05.

How to read it

A higher I at small thresholds indicates very local clustering (tight hotspots).
If I falls as the threshold increases, clustering is primarily local; if I rises, clustering manifests at broader scales.
Significance (permutation p-values) tells you when the observed I departs from random labelings under the given neighborhood definition — use larger permutation counts for formal inference off-line.

Speaker notes / guidance

Use this diagnostic to choose a defensible neighborhood definition for downstream analysis (e.g., LISA or spatial regression).
Do not treat the slide’s small permutation test as a final hypothesis test — rerun with more permutations locally when deciding on significance.
If thresholds produce many isolated units (no neighbors), treat those thresholds with caution: they may distort both I and p-value estimates.

MAUP: Modifiable Areal Unit Problem — story + demo
MAUP: aggregating spatial data into different zoning systems or scales can change patterns and inference. We’ll illustrate by aggregating hex_grid to a coarser grid and comparing maps and Moran’s I.

title: Week 3
text:
Distance-based: code & diagnostics
The code used to generate the diagnostic plot (runs during render). Run with larger permutation counts locally for formal testing.

# (same code as cached block above) compute Moran's I at a few distance thresholds and small permutation p-values
centroids <- st_centroid(hex_grid)
if (st_is_longlat(centroids)) centroids <- st_transform(centroids, 3857)
dm <- st_distance(centroids)
thresholds <- units::set_units(c(25000, 50000, 100000, 200000), "m")
res_list <- lapply(thresholds, function(th) {
  Wd <- (dm <= th) * 1
  diag(Wd) <- 0
  row_sums <- rowSums(Wd)
  Wd[row_sums == 0, ] <- 0
  Wd <- Wd / ifelse(row_sums == 0, 1, row_sums)
  Wd[!is.finite(Wd)] <- 0
  if (sum(Wd) == 0) return(data.frame(dist = as.numeric(th), I = NA_real_, p = NA_real_))
  obsI <- tryCatch(ape::Moran.I(as.numeric(hex_sb), Wd)$observed, error = function(e) NA_real_)
  perms <- replicate(99, tryCatch(ape::Moran.I(sample(as.numeric(hex_sb)), Wd)$observed, error = function(e) NA_real_))
  pval <- (sum(abs(perms) >= abs(obsI), na.rm = TRUE) + 1) / (sum(!is.na(perms)) + 1)
  data.frame(dist = as.numeric(th), I = obsI, p = pval)
})
dfI <- do.call(rbind, res_list)
dfI$dist_km <- dfI$dist / 1000

# show the same plot for transparency
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(dfI, aes(x = dist_km, y = I)) +
  geom_line(color = "#386cb0", size = 0.9) +
  geom_point(aes(color = factor(p < 0.05)), size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(dist_km)), nudge_y = 0.01, size = 3, color = "#444444") +
  scale_color_manual(name = "p < 0.05", values = c("FALSE" = "#fdb462", "TRUE" = "#7fc97f"), na.value = "grey60") +
  xlab("Threshold (km)") + ylab("Moran's I") + theme_minimal() +
  ggtitle("Distance-sensitivity (code-driven)")

title: Week 3
text:
7. Tessellation/MAUP sensitivity

The modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP) is a source of statistical bias that can significantly impact the results of statistical hypothesis tests.
MAUP affects results when point-based measures are aggregated into districts.
The resulting summary values (e.g., totals or proportions) are influenced by both the shape and scale of the aggregation unit.

title: Week 3
text:
1. Why spatial stats?
The central question: Do neighboring observations have similar values?
If YES: - Standard regression breaks (independence assumption violated) - We need spatial statistics to test for clustering and model dependence - The spatial weights matrix W captures neighbor relationships

Why W matters: - Built from geometric relationships: st_touches(), st_intersects(), st_is_within_distance() - Scale depends on tessellation choice (hexagon vs square vs Voronoi) → MAUP - Directly inputs to: Moran’s I, spatial regression (SAR/SEM), LISA, kriging


Section Arc:

Build the neighbor matrix W from geometry (predicates & tessellations)
Test for global clustering with Moran’s I
Visualize local patterns with LISA and spatial-lag plots
Diagnose how spatial dependence breaks OLS and motivates spatial regression

title: Week 3
text:
2. “Near” must be defined

“Near” can be defined in multiple ways; the choice affects neighbor structure and inference.
Common neighbor definitions:

Adjacency: st_touches(), st_intersects() (shared boundary or interior)
Fixed distance: st_is_within_distance() (all units within threshold)
K-nearest: nearest k neighbors (use nngeo::st_nn() or spatial index)
Tessellation-based: Voronoi/Thiessen or grid tiles; adjacency from shared borders

Practical note: ensure CRS/units match when using distance-based neighbors.

title: Week 3
text:
From predicates to neighbors
This is where prior content matters.
We already know how to encode spatial relationships with predicates:

st_touches() → shared borders
st_intersects() → overlap
st_is_within_distance() → distance-based neighbors


These are not just GIS operations.
They are how we turn geometry into a statistical definition of neighborhood.
Key point: the choice of predicate is already a modeling choice.
Water-resources implication: a watershed adjacency rule, stream-network rule, or Euclidean distance rule may imply very different hydrologic processes.

title: Week 3
text:
5. Moran’s I intuition

Moran’s I measures whether similar values cluster in space: conceptually it’s a weighted correlation between a variable and its spatial lag (\(W x\)).
Intuition:

I > 0: similar values cluster (high near high, low near low).
I < 0: neighboring values tend to be dissimilar (high near low).
I ≈ 0: spatial randomness (no detectable autocorrelation).

Quick checks: compare observed I to its expectation under randomness (expected \(\approx -1/(n-1)\)), inspect the Moran scatter (x vs spatial lag) for quadrant structure, and test with permutations for significance.

title: Week 3
text:
6. Moran’s I example
The question: If two hexagons are neighbors, do they have similar Starbucks counts?
Moran’s I is the answer—a test for spatial autocorrelation

Formula (don’t memorize, conceptually: “weighted correlation of X with its spatial lag”):
\[I = \frac{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}(x_i - \bar{x})(x_j - \bar{x})}{σ^2 \sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}}\]
. . . . . .
Our result: I = 0.253, p < 0.001 ✓ Significant positive clustering
What this means: Starbucks are geographically concentrated. Coastal and urban hexagons cluster together; rural hexagons cluster together. This is not a random distribution.

title: Week 3
text:
Local clustering intuition
A global Moran’s I gives one number for the whole map.
A local view asks:

Where are the high-high and low-low areas?


This is a useful bridge to LISA without overloading the first lesson with full local significance testing.
So what? Local patterns are often what matter operationally: where should we investigate, intervene, monitor, or transfer information with caution?

title: Week 3
text:
Dimensionally Extended 9-Intersection Model

The DE-9IM is a topological model and (standard) used to describe the spatial relations of two geometries
Used in geometry, point-set topology, geospatial topology
The DE-9IM matrix provides a way to classify geometry relations using the set {0,1,2,F} or {T,F}
With a {T,F} matrix domain, there are 512 possible relations that can be grouped into binary classification schemes.
About 10 of these, have been given a common name such as intersects, touches, and within.
When testing two geometries against a scheme, the result is a spatial predicate named by the scheme.
Provides the primary basis for queries and assertions in GIS and spatial databases (PostGIS).

title: Week 3
text:
The Matrix Model
The DE-9IM matrix is based on a 3x3 intersection matrix:

Where:

dim is the dimension of the intersection and
I is the interior
B is the boundary
E is the exterior


Empty sets are denoted as F
non-empty sets are denoted with the maximum dimension of the intersection {0,1,2}

Predicate
DE-9IM String Code
Description




Intersects
T*F**FFF*
“Two geometries intersect if they share any portion of space”


Overlaps
T*F**FFF*
“Two geometries overlap if they share some but not all of the same space”


Equals
T*F**FFF*
“Two geometries are topologically equal if their interiors intersect and no part of the interior or boundary of one geometry intersects the exterior of the other”


Disjoint
FF*FF*****
“Two geometries are disjoint: they have no point in common. They form a set of disconnected geometries.”


Touches
FT*******
F**T*****


Contains
T*****FF**
“A contains B: geometry B lies in A, and the interiors intersect”


Covers
T*****FF*
*T****FF*


Within
*T*****FF*
**T****FF*


Covered by
*T*****FF*
**T****FF*

Clipping is a form of subsetting that involves changing the geometry of at least some features.
Clipping can only apply to features more complex than points: (lines, polygons and their ‘multi’ equivalents).

title: Week 3
text:
In cases where we want to reduce the complexity in a geometry we can use simplification algorithms
The most common algorithms are Ramer–Douglas–Peucker and Visvalingam-Whyatt.

title: Week 3
text:
Ramer–Douglas–Peucker

Mark the first and last points as kept
Find the point, p that is the farthest from the first-last line segment. If there are no points between first and last we are done (the base case)
If p is closer than tolerance units to the line segment then everything between first and last can be discarded
Otherwise, mark p as kept and repeat steps 1-4 using the points between first and p and between p and last (the call to recursion)

title: Week 3
text: st_simplify

title: Week 3
text:
st_simplify

sf provides st_simplify, which uses the GEOS implementation of the Douglas-Peucker algorithm to reduce the vertex count.
st_simplify uses the dTolerance to control the level of generalization in map units (see Douglas and Peucker 1973 for details).
Note on CRS: We use EPSG:5070 (USA Contiguous Albers Equal Area projection) for these examples because it preserves area and provides consistent distance measurements across the continental US, making tolerance values meaningful and comparable.

title: Week 3
text:
Performance Impact of Simplification

Simplification dramatically reduces computational complexity for subsequent operations


#> Original points: 11292
#> After 10 km tolerance: 220
#> After 100 km tolerance: 27
#> After 1000 km tolerance: 4

title: Week 3
text:
A limitation with Douglas-Peucker (therefore st_simplify) is that it simplifies objects on a per-geometry basis.
This means the ‘topology’ is lost, resulting in overlapping and disconnected geometries.

title: Week 3
text:
Visvalingam

The Visvalingam algorithm overcomes some limitations of the Douglas-Peucker algorithm (Visvalingam and Whyatt 1993).
it progressively removes points with the least-perceptible change.
Simplification often allows the elimination of 95% or more points while retaining sufficient detail for visualization and often analysis

title: Week 3
text:
Modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP)

The modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP) is a source of statistical bias that can significantly impact the results of statistical hypothesis tests.
MAUP affects results when point-based measures are aggregated into districts.
The resulting summary values (e.g., totals or proportions) are influenced by both the shape and scale of the aggregation unit.

title: Week 3
text:
Worked Example: MAUP with Starbucks

Using the same Starbucks data, aggregating into different grid sizes produces different statistical patterns:


#> Fine grid - Mean: 11.81 SD: 44.57
#> Medium grid - Mean: 45.24 SD: 113.85
#> Coarse grid - Mean: 168.49 SD: 271.16


The spatial patterns and statistical properties differ significantly based on aggregation choice—this is the MAUP!

title: Week 3
text:
Bridge from geometry to inference
So far, we have learned that geometric choices change analysis:

predicates define relationships
tessellations define units
simplification changes representation


Spatial statistics adds one new question:

Do nearby observations tend to have similar values?

If they do, then geometry is not just changing the map — it is changing the inference.

title: Week 3
text:
Why spatial statistics?
Core idea: spatial data are rarely independent.

Nearby places often share similar conditions
Aggregation choices can create or hide pattern
A standard iid mental model can be misleading


So before modeling, we need a formal way to say who is near whom.

title: Week 3
text:
From predicates to neighbors
This is where prior content matters.
We already know how to encode spatial relationships with predicates:

st_touches() → shared borders
st_intersects() → overlap
st_is_within_distance() → distance-based neighbors


These are not just GIS operations.
They are how we turn geometry into a statistical definition of neighborhood.

title: Week 3
text:
Spatial weights matrix W
W is a formal encoding of who counts as near whom.

rows = focal locations
columns = possible neighbors
w_ij > 0 means location j contributes to location i
w_ij = 0 means they are not neighbors


This is the bridge from geometry to spatial inference.

title: Week 3
text:
What W lets us do
Once we have W, we can ask statistical questions about pattern.
Most important first question:

Are nearby values more similar than we would expect by chance?

That is the core idea behind spatial autocorrelation.

For a first pass, the main tool is Moran’s I.

title: Week 3
section: Moran’s I: the first global test
text:
Moran’s I: the first global test
Moran’s I summarizes whether similar values cluster in space.
Interpretation:

positive Moran’s I → similar neighbors cluster together
near 0 → no strong spatial pattern beyond randomness
negative Moran’s I → neighbors tend to be dissimilar


It is a global summary: one value for the whole study area.

title: Week 3
section: A teaching example: Starbucks counts in hexagons
text:
A teaching example: Starbucks counts in hexagons
We will use a simple areal example:

build a hexagon tessellation over CONUS
count Starbucks per hexagon
define neighbors with st_touches()
compute Moran’s I on those counts

title: Week 3
text:
Moran’s I example: map + takeaway

Teaching takeaway: similar values are clustering in space, so the map pattern is not well described as iid randomness.

title: Week 3
section: Spatial lag: what your neighbors look like
text:
Spatial lag: what your neighbors look like
The spatial lag is just the weighted neighbor average:
\[  ext{lag}(x) = W x\]

This gives local intuition: - upper-right = high values near high values - lower-left = low values near low values - off-diagonal = local mismatch / transition

title: Week 3
text:
Local clustering intuition
A global Moran’s I gives one number for the whole map.
A local view asks:

Where are the high-high and low-low areas?


This is a useful bridge to LISA without overloading the first lesson.

title: Week 3

What students should remember

Spatial statistics begin by defining near
Predicates and tessellations create neighbor relationships
Neighbor relationships become the weights matrix W
Moran’s I tests whether similar values cluster globally
Results depend on scale, zoning, and neighborhood definition


That is why geometry matters statistically, not just visually.

What comes next in a fuller course:

We will treat those as extensions, not the main story of this first introduction.

Distance is another way to define neighborhood:
This changes W, so it can also change Moran’s I and local pattern.

title: Week 3
section: Appendix / preview: geostatistics is a different family
text:
Appendix / preview: geostatistics is a different family
Areal autocorrelation asks whether nearby units have similar values.
Geostatistics asks how similarity changes with distance in continuous space.

empirical variogram = summarize semivariance by distance
kriging = use that structure for prediction

For this first lesson, that is enough context.

title: Week 3
section: Standard Regression Fails with Spatial Data
text:
Standard Regression Fails with Spatial Data
OLS Assumption: Observations are independent (residuals are uncorrelated)

Spatial Data Reality: Nearby regions often have correlated attributes - Starbucks density clusters (coastal cities have high density) - Similar urban development patterns - Regional consumer preferences & market saturation - → Residuals are correlated, not independent


Consequences of violating independence:



Problem
Impact




Standard errors too narrow
Over-confident estimates


t-statistics inflated
Too many false positives


95% CI doesn’t cover 95%
Invalid inference


Type I error rate > 5%
Wrong conclusions





Solution: Use spatial statistics that explicitly model dependence - Testing: Moran’s I (test for spatial clustering) - Modeling: Spatial Autoregressive (SAR) or Spatial Error (SEM) models - Interpretation: Spatial lag models, Conditional AutoRegressive (CAR) models

title: Week 3
section: LISA: Which Neighborhoods are Clusters vs. Outliers?
text:
LISA: Which Neighborhoods are Clusters vs. Outliers?
Global Moran’s I = Average clustering across entire region
LISA (Local Indicator of Spatial Association) = Clustering at each location

LISA Quadrants (from Moran scatterplot):


🔴 High-High (red) - High value + high neighbors - Cluster of high values - Example: California coast (high Starbucks, neighbors are high)
🔵 Low-Low (blue) - Low value + low neighbors - Cluster of low values - Example: Rural interior states (low Starbucks, neighbors are low)

🟠 High-Low (orange) - High value + low neighbors - Isolated hotspot (outlier) - Example: Denver metro (high Starbucks surrounded by sparse rural states)
🟢 Low-High (green) - Low value + high neighbors - Rare anomaly - Example: Small town on coast (low local Starbucks but high neighbors)

title: Week 3
text:
In practice: LISA identifies which specific neighborhoods drive the global Moran’s I signal - Are Starbucks clusters concentrated on coasts? Or distributed nationwide? - Are high-density outliers major metros or measurement errors?

#> LISA plots unavailable: tessellation computation not run.

title: Week 3
text:
The Road Ahead: Spatial Regression
Now that you understand spatial dependence, the next step is modeling it

Three spatial regression approaches:

Spatial Autoregressive (SAR):

\(y = \rho W y + X\beta + \epsilon\)
Neighboring values directly influence your value
Best for: Regional spillover effects





Spatial Error (SEM):

\(\epsilon = \lambda W \epsilon + u\)
Omitted variables create correlated errors

Best for: Unobserved heterogeneity





Conditional AutoRegressive (CAR):

Bayesian approach; specific conditional structure
Best for: Spatial smoothing, hierarchical models





You can now look at any spatial dataset and ask: “Are these observations spatially dependent? Which tessellation makes sense? What does that imply for my statistical model?”
You’ll implement these models in Lab-03.

title: Week 3
text:
Dimensionally Extended 9-Intersection Model

The DE-9IM is a topological model and (standard) used to describe the spatial relations of two geometries
Used in geometry, point-set topology, geospatial topology
The DE-9IM matrix provides a way to classify geometry relations using the set {0,1,2,F} or {T,F}
With a {T,F} matrix domain, there are 512 possible relations that can be grouped into binary classification schemes.
About 10 of these, have been given a common name such as intersects, touches, and within.
When testing two geometries against a scheme, the result is a spatial predicate named by the scheme.
Provides the primary basis for queries and assertions in GIS and spatial databases (PostGIS).

title: Week 3
text:
The Matrix Model
The DE-9IM matrix is based on a 3x3 intersection matrix:

Where:

dim is the dimension of the intersection and
I is the interior
B is the boundary
E is the exterior


Empty sets are denoted as F
non-empty sets are denoted with the maximum dimension of the intersection {0,1,2}

Named Predicates

“named spatial predicates” have been defined for some common relations.
A few functions can be derived (expressed by masks) from DE-9IM include (* = wildcard):









Predicate
DE-9IM String Code
Description




Intersects
T*F**FFF*
“Two geometries intersect if they share any portion of space”


Overlaps
T*F**FFF*
“Two geometries overlap if they share some but not all of the same space”


Equals
T*F**FFF*
“Two geometries are topologically equal if their interiors intersect and no part of the interior or boundary of one geometry intersects the exterior of the other”


Disjoint
FF*FF*****
“Two geometries are disjoint: they have no point in common. They form a set of disconnected geometries.”


Touches
FT*******
F**T*****


Contains
T*****FF**
“A contains B: geometry B lies in A, and the interiors intersect”


Covers
T*****FF*
*T****FF*


Within
*T*****FF*
**T****FF*


Covered by
*T*****FF*
**T****FF*

Binary Predicates

Collectively, predicates define the type of relationship each 2D object has with another.
Of the ~ 512 unique relationships offered by the DE-9IM models a selection of ~ 10 have been named.
These are included in PostGIS/GEOS and are made accessible via R sf

st_join

In sf st_join provides this joining capacity
By default, st_join performs a left join (Returns all records from x, and the matched records from y)
It can also do inner joins by setting left = FALSE.
Important: Many-to-many relationships create duplicate rows. In the Starbucks-counties example, a single Starbucks points at a county boundary may match multiple counties, creating multiple rows for that Starbucks.
The default predicate for st_join (and st_filter) is st_intersects, but this can be changed with the .predicate argument to use other spatial relations like st_touches, st_within, etc.
























The default predicate for st_join (and st_filter) is st_intersects
This can be changed with the join argument (see ?st_join for details).

Clipping

Clipping is a form of subsetting that involves changing the geometry of at least some features.
Clipping can only apply to features more complex than points: (lines, polygons and their ‘multi’ equivalents).

Spatial Subsetting

title: Week 3
text:
In cases where we want to reduce the complexity in a geometry we can use simplification algorithms
The most common algorithms are Ramer–Douglas–Peucker and Visvalingam-Whyatt.

title: Week 3
text:
Ramer–Douglas–Peucker

Mark the first and last points as kept
Find the point, p that is the farthest from the first-last line segment. If there are no points between first and last we are done (the base case)
If p is closer than tolerance units to the line segment then everything between first and last can be discarded
Otherwise, mark p as kept and repeat steps 1-4 using the points between first and p and between p and last (the call to recursion)

title: Week 3
text: st_simplify

title: Week 3
text:
st_simplify

sf provides st_simplify, which uses the GEOS implementation of the Douglas-Peucker algorithm to reduce the vertex count.
st_simplify uses the dTolerance to control the level of generalization in map units (see Douglas and Peucker 1973 for details).
Note on CRS: We use EPSG:5070 (USA Contiguous Albers Equal Area projection) for these examples because it preserves area and provides consistent distance measurements across the continental US, making tolerance values meaningful and comparable.

title: Week 3
text:
Performance Impact of Simplification

Simplification dramatically reduces computational complexity for subsequent operations


#> Original points: 11292
#> After 10 km tolerance: 220
#> After 100 km tolerance: 27
#> After 1000 km tolerance: 4

title: Week 3
text:
A limitation with Douglas-Peucker (therefore st_simplify) is that it simplifies objects on a per-geometry basis.
This means the ‘topology’ is lost, resulting in overlapping and disconnected geometries.

title: Week 3
text:
Visvalingam

The Visvalingam algorithm overcomes some limitations of the Douglas-Peucker algorithm (Visvalingam and Whyatt 1993).
it progressively removes points with the least-perceptible change.
Simplification often allows the elimination of 95% or more points while retaining sufficient detail for visualization and often analysis

The ms_simplify function is a wrapper around the mapshaper JavaScript library (created by lead viz experts at the NYT)

Advantages Square Grids

Simple definition and data storage

Only need the origin (lower left), cell size (XY) and grid dimensions

Easy to aggregate and dissaggregate (resample)
Analogous to raster data
Relationship between cells is given
Combining layers is easy with traditional matrix algebra

Advantages Square Grids

Reduced Edge Effects

Lower perimeter to area ratio
minimizes the amount line length needed to create a lattice of cells with a given area

All neighbors are identical

No rook vs queen neighbors

Better fit to curve surfaces (e.g. the earth)

title: Week 3
text:
Triangulations

An alternative to creating equal area tiles is to create triangulations from known anchor points
Triangulation requires a set of input points and seeks to partition the interior into a partition of triangles.
In GIS contexts you’ll hear:

Thiessen Polygon
Voronoi Regions
Delunay Triangulation
TIN (Triangular irregular networks)
etc,..

title: Week 3
text:
Voronoi Polygons

Voronoi/Thiessen polygon boundaries define the area closest to each anchor point relative to all others
They are defined by the perpendicular bisectors of the lines between all points.

title: Week 3
text:
Modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP)

The modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP) is a source of statistical bias that can significantly impact the results of statistical hypothesis tests.
MAUP affects results when point-based measures are aggregated into districts.
The resulting summary values (e.g., totals or proportions) are influenced by both the shape and scale of the aggregation unit.

title: Week 3
text:
Worked Example: MAUP with Starbucks

Using the same Starbucks data, aggregating into different grid sizes produces different statistical patterns:


#> Fine grid - Mean: 11.81 SD: 44.57
#> Medium grid - Mean: 45.24 SD: 113.85
#> Coarse grid - Mean: 168.49 SD: 271.16


The spatial patterns and statistical properties differ significantly based on aggregation choice—this is the MAUP!

title: Week 3
text:
Bridge from geometry to inference
So far, we have learned that geometric choices change analysis:

predicates define relationships
tessellations define units
simplification changes representation


Spatial statistics adds one new question:

Do nearby observations tend to have similar values?

If the answer is yes, then geometry is not just changing the map — it is changing the inference.
Story of this section:

define what “near” means
encode that definition in W
use W to test for clustering
see why changing spatial units can change the answer

title: Week 3
text:
Why spatial statistics?
Core idea: spatial data are rarely independent.

Nearby places often share similar conditions
Aggregation choices can create or hide pattern
A standard iid mental model can be misleading


So before modeling, we need a formal way to say who is near whom.
This is why spatial statistics exists: not because maps are fancy, but because location changes the assumptions behind inference.
So what for water resources?

neighboring catchments often share climate, geology, and land use
nearby gages are rarely independent replicates
flood, drought, and water-quality patterns often organize regionally

title: Week 3
text:
From predicates to neighbors
This is where prior content matters.
We already know how to encode spatial relationships with predicates:

st_touches() → shared borders
st_intersects() → overlap
st_is_within_distance() → distance-based neighbors


These are not just GIS operations.
They are how we turn geometry into a statistical definition of neighborhood.
Key point: the choice of predicate is already a modeling choice.
Water-resources implication: a watershed adjacency rule, stream-network rule, or Euclidean distance rule may imply very different hydrologic processes.

title: Week 3
text:
Spatial weights matrix W
W is a formal encoding of who counts as near whom.

rows = focal locations
columns = possible neighbors
w_ij > 0 means location j contributes to location i
w_ij = 0 means they are not neighbors


This is the bridge from geometry to spatial inference.
So what? If you care about regionalization, transfer learning, model validation, gage networks, or hotspot detection, you are already making choices that belong in W.

title: Week 3
text:
What row-standardizing does
Row-standardizing makes the spatial lag easier to interpret.
Without it:

locations with many neighbors can dominate
raw adjacency counts are harder to compare across space

With it:

each row sums to 1
the lag becomes a weighted average of neighboring values
“my neighborhood signal” becomes directly interpretable

It does not remove the modeling choice — it just makes the choice easier to work with.

title: Week 3
text:
What W lets us do
Once we have W, we can ask statistical questions about pattern.
Most important first question:

Are nearby values more similar than we would expect by chance?

That is the core idea behind spatial autocorrelation.

For a first pass, the main tool is Moran’s I.

title: Week 3
section: Moran’s I: the first global test
text:
Moran’s I: the first global test
Moran’s I summarizes whether similar values cluster in space.
Interpretation:

positive Moran’s I → similar neighbors cluster together
near 0 → no strong spatial pattern beyond randomness
negative Moran’s I → neighbors tend to be dissimilar


It is a global summary: one value for the whole study area.
Mental model: Moran’s I is asking whether values line up with their neighborhood averages more than a random rearrangement would.
Water-resources implication: if streamflow error, nutrient concentration, or flood exposure has strong positive spatial autocorrelation, then nearby units are carrying shared information — and naive independence assumptions can mislead you.

title: Week 3
section: How to read Moran’s I in practice
text:
How to read Moran’s I in practice
When you see a Moran’s I result, ask three questions:

Sign — is the pattern clustered or contrasting?
Magnitude — how strong is the pattern?
Context — what definition of neighborhood produced it?


A Moran’s I value is never just “about the data.” It is always about the data plus the chosen W.

title: Week 3
section: A teaching example: Starbucks counts in hexagons
text:
A teaching example: Starbucks counts in hexagons
We will use a simple areal example:

build a hexagon tessellation over CONUS
count Starbucks per hexagon
define neighbors with st_touches()
compute Moran’s I on those counts

This is a teaching example, not a policy analysis. Its job is to make the statistical logic visible.

title: Week 3
text:
Moran’s I example: map + takeaway

Teaching takeaway: similar values are clustering in space, so this pattern is not well described as iid randomness.
Interpretation in plain English: places with lots of Starbucks tend to be near places with lots of Starbucks; places with few tend to be near places with few.
So what for water resources research?

if flood losses cluster, response planning should be regional, not purely local
if model residuals cluster, validation should account for spatial dependence
if hydrologic signatures cluster, regionalization may be defensible — but only at the right scale

title: Week 3
section: From global pattern to local pattern
text:
From global pattern to local pattern
Moran’s I gives us one number for the whole map.
That is useful, but it hides where the pattern is happening.
To get local intuition, we introduce two related ideas:

the spatial lag: the weighted average of neighboring values
LISA: Local Indicators of Spatial Association


Why this matters:

Moran’s I asks whether clustering exists overall
the spatial lag helps show how each place relates to its neighborhood
LISA asks where local similarity or local contrast is strongest

title: Week 3
section: Spatial lag and LISA: what they are
text:
Spatial lag and LISA: what they are
Spatial lag

for each location, compute a neighborhood summary using W
most often, this is a weighted average of neighboring values
it answers: what do my neighbors look like?

Formula:
\[  ext{lag}(x)_i = \sum_j w_{ij} x_j\]

LISA

stands for Local Indicators of Spatial Association
uses each location’s value together with its neighborhood context
helps identify places that are:

high surrounded by high
low surrounded by low
high surrounded by low
low surrounded by high


For now, think of LISA as the local companion to Moran’s I.

title: Week 3
section: How the spatial lag is calculated
text:
How the spatial lag is calculated
The calculation follows directly from W:

choose a neighborhood definition
build W
take a weighted average of neighbor values for each location


#> counts: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9
#> lag values: 3.67, 3.8, 4.33, 4.6, 5, 5.4, 5.67, 6.2, 6.33


Interpretation:

a high lag means your neighbors tend to have high values
a low lag means your neighbors tend to have low values
comparing your value to your lag helps reveal local agreement or mismatch

Water-resources implication: this is the local logic behind identifying coherent flood-prone regions, drought clusters, unusually impaired reaches, or stations behaving unlike their surroundings.

title: Week 3
section: Spatial lag: what your neighbors look like
text:
Spatial lag: what your neighbors look like
The spatial lag is the weighted neighborhood average:
\[  ext{lag}(x) = W x\]

This gives local intuition:

upper-right = high values near high values
lower-left = low values near low values
off-diagonal = local mismatch or transition

title: Week 3
text:
Why the lag plot matters
The lag plot helps make visible what Moran’s I compresses into one number.

points near the upper-right and lower-left support positive autocorrelation
a diffuse cloud around the center suggests weak structure
strong off-diagonal structure would imply contrast rather than clustering

Start with the global pattern, then look for local structure. That progression makes the map easier to interpret.

title: Week 3
text:
Local clustering intuition
A global Moran’s I gives one number for the whole map.
A local view asks:

Where are the high-high and low-low areas?


This is a useful bridge to LISA without overloading the first lesson with full local significance testing.
So what? Local patterns are often what matter operationally: where should we investigate, intervene, monitor, or transfer information with caution?

title: Week 3

This is the key bridge back to prior content.
The same point data can produce different statistical results when we change the spatial units.

Interpretation: W is not a fact of nature. It depends on the geometry we choose.
Water-resources implication: conclusions about “regional pattern” can change when you move from HUCs to grid cells, from catchments to counties, or from areal neighbors to stream-network neighbors.

title: Week 3
text:
What this means substantively
When tessellation changes, three things can change together:

the number of units
the number of neighbors each unit has
the value of Moran’s I


So a spatial statistic is not just a property of the phenomenon. It is also a property of the representation.
This is why MAUP is not a side note — it is a warning label.
Research takeaway: when your paper makes a spatial claim, you should be ready to explain why your spatial units and neighborhood rule are substantively defensible.

title: Week 3
text:
Common beginner mistakes

Treating W as obvious or neutral
Reporting Moran’s I without explaining the neighborhood rule
Moving from one global statistic straight to causal claims
Forgetting that aggregation choice can change the result

Safer habit: always describe how neighbors were defined and why that definition is substantively reasonable.
In water resources research, this means: tie your spatial definition back to process — flow connectivity, basin similarity, meteorology, infrastructure, administration, or management scale.

title: Week 3
text:
What students should remember

Spatial statistics begin by defining near
Predicates and tessellations create neighbor relationships
Neighbor relationships become the weights matrix W
Moran’s I tests whether similar values cluster globally
Results depend on scale, zoning, and neighborhood definition


That is why geometry matters statistically, not just visually.
Bottom line for water resources: spatial statistics helps you decide whether apparent regional pattern is signal, artifact, or some mixture of both.

title: Week 3
text:
Preview, not mastery
Today’s core lesson is:

global autocorrelation: Moran’s I
local clustering intuition: lag quadrants / LISA preview
sensitivity to spatial representation: MAUP

What comes next in a fuller course:

spatial regression
distance-threshold sensitivity
Geary’s C
variograms
kriging

We will treat those as extensions, not the main story of this first introduction.

title: Week 3
text:
Two defensible ways to define “near”
A shared-border rule is not the only option.

contiguity neighbors: units touch along an edge or boundary
distance neighbors: units are within some threshold distance


Both are reasonable in different settings. Changing this choice changes W, and that can change Moran’s I.

title: Week 3
section: Appendix / preview: geostatistics is a different family
text:
Appendix / preview: geostatistics is a different family
Areal autocorrelation asks whether nearby units have similar values.
Geostatistics asks how similarity changes with distance in continuous space.

empirical variogram = summarize semivariance by distance
kriging = use that structure for prediction

For this first lesson, the main point is just that these are related, but not identical, branches of spatial statistics.

title: Week 3
section: Standard Regression Fails with Spatial Data
text:
Standard Regression Fails with Spatial Data
OLS Assumption: Observations are independent (residuals are uncorrelated)

Spatial Data Reality: Nearby regions often have correlated attributes

Starbucks density clusters (coastal cities have high density)
Similar urban development patterns
Regional consumer preferences & market saturation
→ Residuals are correlated, not independent



Consequences of violating independence:



Problem
Impact




Standard errors too narrow
Over-confident estimates


t-statistics inflated
Too many false positives


95% CI doesn’t cover 95%
Invalid inference


Type I error rate > 5%
Wrong conclusions





Solution: Use spatial statistics that explicitly model dependence

Testing: Moran’s I (test for spatial clustering)
Modeling: Spatial Autoregressive (SAR) or Spatial Error (SEM) models
Interpretation: Spatial lag models, Conditional AutoRegressive (CAR) models

title: Week 3
section: LISA: Which Neighborhoods are Clusters vs. Outliers?
text:
LISA: Which Neighborhoods are Clusters vs. Outliers?
Global Moran’s I = Average clustering across entire region
LISA (Local Indicator of Spatial Association) = Clustering at each location

LISA Quadrants (from Moran scatterplot):


🔴 High-High (red)

High value + high neighbors
Cluster of high values
Example: California coast (high Starbucks, neighbors are high)

🔵 Low-Low (blue)

Low value + low neighbors
Cluster of low values
Example: Rural interior states (low Starbucks, neighbors are low)


🟠 High-Low (orange)

High value + low neighbors
Isolated hotspot (outlier)
Example: Denver metro (high Starbucks surrounded by sparse rural states)

🟢 Low-High (green)

Low value + high neighbors
Rare anomaly
Example: Small town on coast (low local Starbucks but high neighbors)

title: Week 3
text:
In practice: LISA identifies which specific neighborhoods drive the global Moran’s I signal

Are Starbucks clusters concentrated on coasts? Or distributed nationwide?
Are high-density outliers major metros or measurement errors?


#> LISA plots unavailable: tessellation computation not run.

title: Week 3
text:
The Road Ahead: Spatial Regression
Now that you understand spatial dependence, the next step is modeling it

Three spatial regression approaches:

Spatial Autoregressive (SAR):

\(y = \rho W y + X\beta + \epsilon\)
Neighboring values directly influence your value
Best for: Regional spillover effects





Spatial Error (SEM):

\(\epsilon = \lambda W \epsilon + u\)
Omitted variables create correlated errors

Best for: Unobserved heterogeneity





Conditional AutoRegressive (CAR):

Bayesian approach; specific conditional structure
Best for: Spatial smoothing, hierarchical models





You can now look at any spatial dataset and ask: “Are these observations spatially dependent? Which tessellation makes sense? What does that imply for my statistical model?”
You’ll implement these models in Lab-03.

title: Week 3
text:
Example: Starbucks counts in hexagons
We will use a simple areal example:

build a hexagon tessellation over CONUS
count Starbucks per hexagon
define neighbors with st_touches()
compute Moran’s I on those counts

This example is simplified, not definitive. Its purpose is to make the statistical logic visible before moving to real research settings.

title: Week 3
text:
Key takeaways

Spatial statistics begin by defining near
Predicates and tessellations create neighbor relationships
Neighbor relationships become the weights matrix W
Moran’s I tests whether similar values cluster globally
Results depend on scale, zoning, and neighborhood definition


That is why geometry matters statistically, not just visually.
Bottom line for water resources: spatial statistics helps you decide whether apparent regional pattern is signal, artifact, or some mixture of both.

title: Lab 3: Answer Key — A+ Student Exemplar
text:
Step 2.5 — Commentary on MAUP implications
A+ Student Analysis:
The tessellation comparison reveals the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem (MAUP) in action across two dimensions:
1. Heterogeneity (Scale Effect)

Counties (heterogeneity_index = 3.217): Highly variable due to historical/political boundaries. Large counties (e.g., Nevada’s Lander County: 17,500 km²) dwarf small urban counties (New York’s New York County: 63 km²). This variability biases spatial analysis toward large regions.
Regular grids (hexagons CV = 0.008; squares CV = 0.011): Perfectly uniform tiles make spatial comparisons equitable—each tile contributes equally regardless of location. This eliminates scale bias inherent in county data.
Tessellations (Voronoi CV = 1.489; Triangles CV = 0.896): Intermediate heterogeneity. Voronoi cells near boundaries become very large; triangulation produces more uniform sizes but still variable.

2. Implications for Dam Analysis
If we analyze dam counts per county, large counties (low density) and small counties (high density) will have vastly different counts regardless of true spatial clustering. A dam manager might conclude “that Nevada county is sparse” simply because Nevada is geographically vast, not because dams are actually dispersed.
Constant-area tessellations (hexagon/square grids) remove this confound. A hexagon with 50 dams shows genuine clustering; a nearby hexagon with 5 dams is genuinely sparse—both represent the same geographic scale.
3. Computational Efficiency Trade-off

Computationally simple: Regular grids are O(n) for spatial joins
Computationally complex: County joins require topology checks on irregular boundaries
For this analysis, hexagons chosen: 1,921 regular tiles with uniform neighborhoods (6 neighbors each) provide stable spatial analysis without the computational burden of 3,108 county geometries

4. MAUP in Practice
A hypothetical example: Suppose real dam clustering exists only in Arizona (concentrated in Salt River, Colorado River systems). Using counties, this might appear as variable clustering across 4–6 large Arizona counties. Using a hexagon grid, it emerges as 3–4 adjacent hotspot hexagons, revealing the true spatial pattern more clearly. Different tessellations don’t invalidate results—they reveal different scales of organization.
Recommendation: For policy analysis, choose tessellations aligned with management units. For dam infrastructure (multi-state basins), hexagons at n=70 (~1,900 tiles, ~500 km² per tile) approximates basin-scale coordination regions—meaningful for policy.

text:
Step 3.2 — Create point-in-polygon function

# A+ Student's robust, well-documented function
count_dams_in_tiles <- function(dams_sf, tiles_sf, id_col_name) {
  
  # Spatial join: each dam → nearest/containing tile
  # st_join uses st_intersects by default (dam is in tile)
  dams_joined <- st_join(dams_sf, tiles_sf %>% select(all_of(id_col_name)))
  
  # Count dams per tile ID
  dam_counts <- dams_joined %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    group_by(across(all_of(id_col_name))) %>%
    summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop")
  
  # Left join back to tessellation to preserve empty tiles
  # Important: empty tiles (n = 0) must appear for accurate spatial analysis
  result <- tiles_sf %>%
    left_join(dam_counts, by = id_col_name) %>%
    replace_na(list(n = 0))
  
  return(result)
}

# Test function

A+ Implementation Notes: - Uses left join to preserve empty tiles (critical for spatial analysis—you can’t ignore ~30% of your domain!) - Drops geometry after join, then re-joins to avoid duplicating geometry columns - Uses tidy evaluation ({ }) to accept column names programmatically - Includes validation output so student can verify no dams were lost

Regional Analysis - Where Tessellation Choice Matters:

Tennessee Valley (TVA Region):

Counties show 5–8 counties with high dam counts, unclear if this is clustering or political boundary artifact
Hexagons show 4–6 adjacent hotspot hexagons in clear dam-concentrating region
Interpretation: Hexagons reveal true clustering; counties confuse political boundaries with infrastructure patterns
Why: Regular hexagon boundaries align with hydrologic flow patterns (river systems) better than county lines

Colorado River Basin:

Counties show extreme heterogeneity: Nevada (large, low density) vs. Arizona (fragmented, high density)
Hexagons show consistent ~15–20 dams per cell across both states
Interpretation: Hexagons reveal that dam density is actually similar across state lines—policy coordination is geographically coherent, not state-dependent
Why: Equal-area hexagons eliminate the Nevada-size-distortion problem

Mountain West (Sparse Region):

Counties: Many large, empty counties create visual “dead zones”
Hexagons: Same sparsity shown as empty hexagons (0 dams)—pattern is clearer
Interpretation: Equally spaces empty tiles vs. huge empty counties both communicate sparsity, but hexagons are easier to parse visually


Justification:

Aligns with management: River basins and water-sharing compacts cross state lines. Hexagonal tessellation at n=70 (~1,900 km² per tile) represents multi-state coordination regions.
Eliminates MAUP confusion: Regular geometry eliminates the scale-effect bias that plagued county data. No misinterpretation of cluster vs. boundary artifact.
Computational stability: Uniform neighbors (6 per hexagon) enables consistent spatial analysis. No isolated tiles, no neighborhood size variation.
Simplification trade-off: At keep=0.08, 22.5× computational speedup with visually acceptable coastlines.

Why Not Others:

Counties: MAUP nightmare; area heterogeneity (3,200×) biases counts
Voronoi: Boundary cells explode in size; unstable for edge analyses
Triangles: 6,196 tiles → over-fragmentation; noisy local variation dominates signal
Squares: Acceptable alternative (equally valid), but:

Only 4 neighbors per cell → less stable spatial neighbor estimates
Cardinal orientation (N/S/E/W bias) can align with political boundaries (state lines run N/S in Western US, creating artificial patterns)


Did Simplification Affect Choice?
At keep=0.08, we lost ~92% of boundary vertices but retained all major geographic features. Coarser simplification (keep=0.05) slightly distorted Great Lakes and caused dams on Lake Superior borders to be incorrectly filtered. Finer simplification (keep=0.10) added ~5 seconds computation with no visual/analytical improvement. keep=0.08 is justified as Pareto-optimal: best practical balance.

title: Lab 3: Answer Key
text:
Step 6.3 — Interpretation (Rubric for Students)
Students should address all of the following:

Tessellation variation: Expected I ≈ 0.35–0.45 for all three, with variation ±0.03. This minimal variation indicates the clustering signal is robust—not an artifact of tessellation choice.
Statistical significance: All three tessellations should show p < 0.05, indicating genuine positive spatial autocorrelation. Neighboring tiles have significantly similar dam counts, not random variation.
Calibration: Compare your results to expected ranges for infrastructure clustering:

Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) region: I ≈ 0.50–0.65 (very strong clustering)
Western water systems (Colorado, California): I ≈ 0.35–0.50 (strong clustering)
Random/dispersed infrastructure: I ≈ 0.05–0.15 (weak)

If your hexagon I ≈ 0.38, p < 0.05, this aligns with real-world infrastructure clustering patterns.
Why tessellation choice matters: Regular tessellations (hex, square) have uniform neighbor counts (6, 4 respectively), producing stable I estimates. Voronoi has variable neighbors (3–8), potentially affecting stability. For policy decisions, both are defensible; for statistical rigor, regular grids are preferable.
MAUP insight (most critical): Different tessellations define “neighbors” differently. Using identical dam data:

Hexagon: Neighbors share hexagon boundaries
Square: Neighbors share square boundaries
Voronoi: Neighbors share Voronoi cell boundaries

A policy maker receiving reports from different tessellations could reach different conclusions about clustering severity—all correct within their geometry. By grounding tessellation choice in policy questions (basin-scale coordination → hexagons), you learn that MAUP is not a weakness to hide, but a parameter you consciously control.

title: Lab 3: Answer Key
text:
Common Errors to Watch For

Neighbor matrix construction (Q6.1):

Forgetting diag() <- 0 creates self-loops, artificially inflates I
Not row-standardizing weights biases I toward high-neighbor regions
rowSums(W) == 0 for isolated tiles creates Inf; use W[!is.finite(W)] <- 0

Moran’s I interpretation (Q6.3):

Confusing “significant I” with “strong clustering” (I = 0.35, p < 0.05 is significant but moderate, not “strong”)
Misinterpreting p-value: p < 0.05 means “unlikely to be random,” not “strong magnitude”
Recommending finer tessellations to increase I (wrong—smaller tiles change I, don’t inherently improve it)

Simplification (Q5):

Applying simplified boundary to tessellation coordinates (wrong—simplification is only for clipping)
Using very coarse simplification (keep < 0.05) and getting > 1% area loss, then declaring it “too aggressive”
No verification step—students should visually overlay results

Point-in-polygon (Q3):

Forgetting to assign dams to tiles with no points (those should appear with n = 0 if using left_join)
Using inner_join instead of left_join, losing empty tiles

hexagon_clipped <- st_filter(hexagon_grid, usa_simplified)

title: Lab 3: Answer Key
text:
Common Student Errors

NA propagation: If many tiles have zero dams, NAs in spatial lag cause correlation to fail. Students must impute before lag calculation, then correlate only where original data exists.
Misinterpreting correlation strength:

r = 0.35 with p < 0.05 is “significant but weak” clustering
Students often confuse p-value with effect size

Tessellation sensitivity: Students sometimes conclude “hexagons give different results than squares, so LISA is invalid.” Correct interpretation: “Different tessellations yield slightly different quadrant counts, which is expected (MAUP); magnitude of HH/LL patterns is robust.”
OLS violation threshold: No hard rule for “when is r large enough to warrant spatial regression.” Guidance: r > 0.50 is strong signal; r = 0.30–0.50 is ambiguous (both OLS and spatial regression defensible); r < 0.20 suggests independence is reasonable.
