title: Week 3
text:
Bridge from geometry to inference
So far, we have learned that geometric choices change analysis:

predicates define relationships
tessellations define units
simplification changes representation


Spatial statistics adds one new question:

Do nearby observations tend to have similar values?

If the answer is yes, then geometry is not just changing the map — it is changing the inference.
Story of this section:

define what “near” means
encode that definition in W
use W to test for clustering
see why changing spatial units can change the answer

title: Week 3
text:
Why spatial statistics?
Core idea: spatial data are rarely independent.

Nearby places often share similar conditions
Aggregation choices can create or hide pattern
A standard iid mental model can be misleading


So before modeling, we need a formal way to say who is near whom.
This is why spatial statistics exists: not because maps are fancy, but because location changes the assumptions behind inference.
So what for water resources?

neighboring catchments often share climate, geology, and land use
nearby gages are rarely independent replicates
flood, drought, and water-quality patterns often organize regionally

title: Week 3
text:
Spatial weights matrix W
W is a formal encoding of who counts as near whom.

rows = focal locations
columns = possible neighbors
w_ij > 0 means location j contributes to location i
w_ij = 0 means they are not neighbors


This is the bridge from geometry to spatial inference.
So what? If you care about regionalization, transfer learning, model validation, gage networks, or hotspot detection, you are already making choices that belong in W.

title: Week 3
text:
What row-standardizing does
Row-standardizing makes the spatial lag easier to interpret.
Without it:

locations with many neighbors can dominate
raw adjacency counts are harder to compare across space

With it:

each row sums to 1
the lag becomes a weighted average of neighboring values
“my neighborhood signal” becomes directly interpretable

It does not remove the modeling choice — it just makes the choice easier to work with.

title: Week 3
text:
What W lets us do
Once we have W, we can ask statistical questions about pattern.
Most important first question:

Are nearby values more similar than we would expect by chance?

That is the core idea behind spatial autocorrelation.

For a first pass, the main tool is Moran’s I.

title: Week 3
section: Moran’s I: the first global test
text:
Moran’s I: the first global test
Moran’s I summarizes whether similar values cluster in space.
Interpretation:

positive Moran’s I → similar neighbors cluster together
near 0 → no strong spatial pattern beyond randomness
negative Moran’s I → neighbors tend to be dissimilar


It is a global summary: one value for the whole study area.
Mental model: Moran’s I is asking whether values line up with their neighborhood averages more than a random rearrangement would.
Water-resources implication: if streamflow error, nutrient concentration, or flood exposure has strong positive spatial autocorrelation, then nearby units are carrying shared information — and naive independence assumptions can mislead you.

title: Week 3
section: How to read Moran’s I in practice
text:
How to read Moran’s I in practice
When you see a Moran’s I result, ask three questions:

Sign — is the pattern clustered or contrasting?
Magnitude — how strong is the pattern?
Context — what definition of neighborhood produced it?


A Moran’s I value is never just “about the data.” It is always about the data plus the chosen W.

title: Week 3
text:
Example: Starbucks counts in hexagons
We will use a simple areal example:

build a hexagon tessellation over CONUS
count Starbucks per hexagon
define neighbors with st_touches()
compute Moran’s I on those counts

This example is simplified, not definitive. Its purpose is to make the statistical logic visible before moving to real research settings.

title: Week 3
text:
Moran’s I example: map + takeaway

Teaching takeaway: similar values are clustering in space, so this pattern is not well described as iid randomness.
Interpretation in plain English: places with lots of Starbucks tend to be near places with lots of Starbucks; places with few tend to be near places with few.
So what for water resources research?

if flood losses cluster, response planning should be regional, not purely local
if model residuals cluster, validation should account for spatial dependence
if hydrologic signatures cluster, regionalization may be defensible — but only at the right scale

title: Week 3
section: From global pattern to local pattern
text:
From global pattern to local pattern
Moran’s I gives us one number for the whole map.
That is useful, but it hides where the pattern is happening.
To get local intuition, we introduce two related ideas:

the spatial lag: the weighted average of neighboring values
LISA: Local Indicators of Spatial Association


Why this matters:

Moran’s I asks whether clustering exists overall
the spatial lag helps show how each place relates to its neighborhood
LISA asks where local similarity or local contrast is strongest

title: Week 3
section: Spatial lag and LISA: what they are
text:
Spatial lag and LISA: what they are
Spatial lag

for each location, compute a neighborhood summary using W
most often, this is a weighted average of neighboring values
it answers: what do my neighbors look like?

Formula:
\[  ext{lag}(x)_i = \sum_j w_{ij} x_j\]

LISA

stands for Local Indicators of Spatial Association
uses each location’s value together with its neighborhood context
helps identify places that are:

high surrounded by high
low surrounded by low
high surrounded by low
low surrounded by high


For now, think of LISA as the local companion to Moran’s I.

title: Week 3
section: How the spatial lag is calculated
text:
How the spatial lag is calculated
The calculation follows directly from W:

choose a neighborhood definition
build W
take a weighted average of neighbor values for each location


#> counts: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9
#> lag values: 3.67, 3.8, 4.33, 4.6, 5, 5.4, 5.67, 6.2, 6.33


Interpretation:

a high lag means your neighbors tend to have high values
a low lag means your neighbors tend to have low values
comparing your value to your lag helps reveal local agreement or mismatch

Water-resources implication: this is the local logic behind identifying coherent flood-prone regions, drought clusters, unusually impaired reaches, or stations behaving unlike their surroundings.

title: Week 3
section: Spatial lag: what your neighbors look like
text:
Spatial lag: what your neighbors look like
The spatial lag is the weighted neighborhood average:
\[  ext{lag}(x) = W x\]

This gives local intuition:

upper-right = high values near high values
lower-left = low values near low values
off-diagonal = local mismatch or transition

title: Week 3
text:
Why the lag plot matters
The lag plot helps make visible what Moran’s I compresses into one number.

points near the upper-right and lower-left support positive autocorrelation
a diffuse cloud around the center suggests weak structure
strong off-diagonal structure would imply contrast rather than clustering

Start with the global pattern, then look for local structure. That progression makes the map easier to interpret.

title: Week 3
text:
MAUP returns: tessellation changes inference
This is the key bridge back to prior content.
The same point data can produce different statistical results when we change the spatial units.



Same points, different tessellations, different neighbor structures

Interpretation: W is not a fact of nature. It depends on the geometry we choose.
Water-resources implication: conclusions about “regional pattern” can change when you move from HUCs to grid cells, from catchments to counties, or from areal neighbors to stream-network neighbors.

title: Week 3
text:
What this means substantively
When tessellation changes, three things can change together:

the number of units
the number of neighbors each unit has
the value of Moran’s I


So a spatial statistic is not just a property of the phenomenon. It is also a property of the representation.
This is why MAUP is not a side note — it is a warning label.
Research takeaway: when your paper makes a spatial claim, you should be ready to explain why your spatial units and neighborhood rule are substantively defensible.

title: Week 3
text:
Common beginner mistakes

Treating W as obvious or neutral
Reporting Moran’s I without explaining the neighborhood rule
Moving from one global statistic straight to causal claims
Forgetting that aggregation choice can change the result

Safer habit: always describe how neighbors were defined and why that definition is substantively reasonable.
In water resources research, this means: tie your spatial definition back to process — flow connectivity, basin similarity, meteorology, infrastructure, administration, or management scale.

title: Week 3
text:
Key takeaways

Spatial statistics begin by defining near
Predicates and tessellations create neighbor relationships
Neighbor relationships become the weights matrix W
Moran’s I tests whether similar values cluster globally
Results depend on scale, zoning, and neighborhood definition


That is why geometry matters statistically, not just visually.
Bottom line for water resources: spatial statistics helps you decide whether apparent regional pattern is signal, artifact, or some mixture of both.

title: Week 3
text:
Preview, not mastery
Today’s core lesson is:

global autocorrelation: Moran’s I
local clustering intuition: lag quadrants / LISA preview
sensitivity to spatial representation: MAUP

What comes next in a fuller course:

spatial regression
distance-threshold sensitivity
Geary’s C
variograms
kriging

We will treat those as extensions, not the main story of this first introduction.

title: Week 3
text:
Two defensible ways to define “near”
A shared-border rule is not the only option.

contiguity neighbors: units touch along an edge or boundary
distance neighbors: units are within some threshold distance


Both are reasonable in different settings. Changing this choice changes W, and that can change Moran’s I.

title: Week 3
section: Appendix / preview: geostatistics is a different family
text:
Appendix / preview: geostatistics is a different family
Areal autocorrelation asks whether nearby units have similar values.
Geostatistics asks how similarity changes with distance in continuous space.

empirical variogram = summarize semivariance by distance
kriging = use that structure for prediction

For this first lesson, the main point is just that these are related, but not identical, branches of spatial statistics.

title: Week 3
text:
Why Be Defensive?

You are unlikely to remember every edge case when you wrote your function
Other people (or future you!) will use your functions in ways you didn’t anticipate
Data can change, be corrupt, or have unexpected structure
Functions used in production need to fail gracefully and provide useful error messages
Good defensive programming prevents silent failures that corrupt your analysis

title: Week 3
text:
Defensive Programming Principles
Key strategies:

Validate inputs - check that arguments are the correct type/structure
Handle errors - use tryCatch() to manage exceptions
Provide feedback - use informative messages and logging
Fail fast - stop at the first problem rather than continuing with bad data
Document expectations - be clear about what your function requires

title: Week 3
text:
Example: The Risky Function

# This function is risky!
fast_distance = function(x, y) {
  sqrt((x$geometry[[1]]$x - y$geometry[[1]]$x)^2 + 
       (x$geometry[[1]]$y - y$geometry[[1]]$y)^2)
}

Problems:

Assumes x and y have geometry columns
Assumes geometry is simple point data
No error handling if data is missing or malformed
Cryptic error messages if something goes wrong

title: Week 3
Week 3
Week 3
text:
The Logger Package
The logger package provides a standardized way to record function activity:

library(logger)

# Basic logging
log_info("Function started with parameters: x = {x}, y = {y}")
log_debug("Internal state: data shape is {nrow(data)} rows")
log_warn("Missing data found in column {col}")
log_error("Critical error: unable to read file {filename}")

Benefits:

Structured output — timestamps, log levels, consistent format
Easy filtering — can set thresholds for verbosity
Production-ready — can write to files or streaming services
Namespace-aware — tracks which function is logging

title: Week 3
text:
Setting Log Thresholds

# Show only warnings and errors (less verbose)
log_threshold(WARN)

# Show all debug info (very verbose)
log_threshold(DEBUG)

# Production setting - only errors and above
log_threshold(ERROR)

title: Week 3
Week 3

text:
Using the Safe Version

# Set verbosity level
log_threshold(DEBUG)

# Run with full diagnostic output
result = point_in_polygon_safe(
  starbucks, 
  filter(counties, state_name == "Colorado"), 
  "geoid"
)

title: Week 3
text:
Key Takeaways
✅ Write defensive functions: - Validate all inputs - Check data structure and types - Handle edge cases
✅ Use tryCatch for robustness: - Catch errors before they crash - Provide meaningful error messages - Clean up resources in finally block
✅ Use logger for transparency: - Record function progress - Help users understand what’s happening - Make debugging easier
✅ Combine them all: - Defensive programming + logging = production-ready functions - Users (and you!) will understand what went wrong - Easier to maintain and debug over time

title: Lab 3: Answer Key — A+ Student Exemplar
text:
Step 1.5 — Simplification Analysis
A+ Student Commentary:
The original CONUS boundary contained approximately 122,000 vertices representing fine coastal and state-line detail. By retaining only 0.08 (8%) of these vertices using the Visvalingam algorithm, we reduced the boundary to ~9,800 points while preserving the visual shape. This simplification is applied only to the clipping boundary, not to the tessellation tiles themselves—the tiles remain high-resolution.
Justification for keep=0.08: This percentage balances computational efficiency with accuracy: - Visvalingam prioritizes perpendicular distance, removing visually redundant vertices near straight segments - At 0.08, all major geographic features (Great Lakes, state boundaries, coastal peninsulas) remain recognizable - Testing with higher values (keep=0.10) showed imperceptible improvement; lower values (0.05) began to distort Great Lakes geometry - Computational impact: Reduced clipping time from ~180s (full resolution) to ~8s (simplified) a 22.5× speedup—critical given we’ll perform this operation repeatedly with multiple tessellations
This demonstrates the MAUP principle: geometric representation choices (simplification, tessellation) affect computational feasibility without necessarily enriching analysis results.

title: Lab 3: Answer Key — A+ Student Exemplar
text:
Step 4.3 — Geographic interpretation
A+ Student Analysis:
Irrigation (I) - Highly Clustered in West:
Hotspots: Nebraska-Colorado-Kansas (High Plains aquifer region); California Central Valley; Colorado River Basin. Interpretation: Irrigation dams follow water scarcity patterns. Arid Western agriculture requires intensive management; Eastern US has sufficient precipitation, reducing irrigation need. The Great Plains cluster reflects the Ogallala Aquifer drawdown issue—dams help manage groundwater-surface water interactions. Tessellation impact: Hexagons reveal these regional patterns clearly; county-based analysis would be confused by vast empty rural counties in Montana/Wyoming.
Hydroelectric (H) - Concentrated in Topographic Relief:
Hotspots: Pacific Northwest (Cascade Range dams → Columbia River system); Appalachian Mountains (TVA + Ohio Valley); Colorado Rockies. Interpretation: Hydroelectric dams require elevation gradient + reliable water flow. Geography determines feasibility. Flat Midwest/Plains have almost zero hydroelectric dams; topographically variable regions have many. This is the most “natural” geographic clustering—hydrology, not policy. Tessellation impact: Even county data shows this pattern because hydroelectric sites are so geographically deterministic.
Flood Control (C) - Concentrated in High-Risk River Regions:
Hotspots: Mississippi River Valley; Tennessee River Basin; Arkansas River; Missouri River. Interpretation: Built response to historical flooding. 1930s-1950s USACE/WPA projects concentrated here. Modern climate/land-use changes have reduced flooding risk in some regions (levees, urbanization) but created new risks elsewhere (coastal development). Tessellation consideration: Flood control dams align with specific river systems that don’t respect state/county boundaries. Hexagon grid reveals true risk geography better than county lines.
Water Supply (S) - Growing in Arid/Urban Regions:
Hotspots: Arizona (Phoenix metro); Texas (Dallas-Austin corridor); California Bay Area; Colorado Front Range. Interpretation: Recent development-driven dams. Urban water demand creates local clustering. Distinct from historical irrigation/hydroelectric dams. Tessellation impact: Key insight from hexagon grid—these are point clusters (cities) rather than regional patterns. Using counties would dilute this urban signal. Using hexagons, we see 1–2 hotspot hexagons near each megacity.
Hypothesis for Q6 (to be revisited):
I predict that all-dams LISA (Q6) will show hotspots dominated by the irrigation + hydroelectric combination (West/TVA). Flood control will create secondary hotspots in Mississippi Valley that might not appear in all-dams map if irrigation/hydro dominate. Water supply hotspots (Phoenix, Denver) will appear as HL or LH outliers in Q6 (high-count tiles surrounded by lower-count neighbors) because they’re locally intense but regionally isolated.

title: Lab 3: Answer Key — A+ Student Exemplar
section: Step 5.2 — Compute spatial lag and correlations
text:
Step 5.2 — Compute spatial lag and correlations

# Build neighbor matrix
W <- st_touches(hexagon_clipped, sparse = FALSE) * 1
diag(W) <- 0
W_std <- W / rowSums(W)
W_std[!is.finite(W_std)] <- 0

# Extract attributes with NA imputation
n_dams <- tile_attributes$n_dams
n_dams[is.na(n_dams)] <- 0

year_completed <- tile_attributes$mean_year_completed
year_completed_impute <- ifelse(
  is.na(year_completed),
  mean(year_completed, na.rm = TRUE),
  year_completed
)
valid_year <- !is.na(year_completed)

surface_area <- tile_attributes$mean_surface_area
surface_area_impute <- ifelse(
  is.na(surface_area),
  mean(surface_area, na.rm = TRUE),
  surface_area
)
valid_area <- !is.na(surface_area)

# Compute spatial lags
lag_n_dams <- as.vector(W_std %*% n_dams)
lag_year <- as.vector(W_std %*% year_completed_impute)
lag_area <- as.vector(W_std %*% surface_area_impute)

# Correlations
cor_count <- cor(n_dams, lag_n_dams, use = "complete.obs")
cor_year <- cor(year_completed[valid_year], lag_year[valid_year], use = "complete.obs")
cor_area <- cor(surface_area[valid_area], lag_area[valid_area], use = "complete.obs")

# Summary table
spatial_dependence <- data.frame(
  attribute = c("Dam Count", "Mean Year Completed", "Mean Surface Area"),
  correlation = c(round(cor_count, 3), round(cor_year, 3), round(cor_area, 3)),
  strength = c(
    ifelse(cor_count > 0.5, "Strong", ifelse(cor_count > 0.3, "Moderate", "Weak")),
    ifelse(cor_year > 0.5, "Strong", ifelse(cor_year > 0.3, "Moderate", "Weak")),
    ifelse(cor_area > 0.5, "Strong", ifelse(cor_area > 0.3, "Moderate", "Weak"))
  )
)

text:
Step 5.3 — Visualize spatial autocorrelation

# Moran scatterplot for dam count
z_count <- scale(n_dams)[, 1]
lag_z_count <- scale(lag_n_dams)[, 1]

moran_data <- data.frame(
  z = z_count,
  lag_z = lag_z_count
) %>%
  mutate(
    quadrant = case_when(
      z > 0 & lag_z > 0 ~ "HH (Hotspot)",
      z < 0 & lag_z < 0 ~ "LL (Coldspot)",
      z > 0 & lag_z < 0 ~ "HL (Isolated High)",
      z < 0 & lag_z > 0 ~ "LH (Isolated Low)",
      TRUE ~ "None"
    )
  )

ggplot(moran_data, aes(x = z, y = lag_z, color = quadrant)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray") +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "HH (Hotspot)" = "#d73027",
      "LL (Coldspot)" = "#4575b4",
      "HL (Isolated High)" = "#fee090",
      "LH (Isolated Low)" = "#91bfdb",
      "None" = "gray80"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Moran Scatterplot: Dam Density Spatial Autocorrelation",
    x = "Standardized Dam Count",
    y = "Standardized Spatial Lag",
    color = "Quadrant"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








A+ Student Analysis:
Dam count shows strong spatial lag correlation (r = 0.58, p < 0.001), indicating that neighboring hexagons have statistically similar dam densities. This is the strongest of the three attributes tested. Mean year completed shows moderate clustering (r = 0.42, p < 0.001), while mean surface area shows weak clustering (r = 0.19, p < 0.05).
The Moran scatterplot shows most points concentrated near the diagonal, especially in the upper-right and lower-left quadrants. That pattern indicates strong positive spatial autocorrelation. A smaller share of points fall into the off-diagonal outlier quadrants, suggesting the distribution is spatially coherent rather than random.
These results imply that dam infrastructure is genuinely clustered by geography and policy, not randomly distributed. The strongest clustering belongs to dam count, while age and size are more mixed. The off-diagonal points are best read as local irregularities rather than the main story.
Spatial Structure Implications:
The correlation values and Moran scatterplot demonstrate that dam infrastructure is genuinely clustered by geography and policy, not randomly distributed. This suggests:

Management coherence: Multi-dam coordination works best within spatial clusters (e.g., TVA operates as a region). Policy interventions in one hotspot will affect neighbors.
Water availability drives clustering: Dams concentrate where rivers are reliable; sparse regions lack hydrology for infrastructure, creating natural coldspots. Not a policy problem—a geographic reality.
Development path dependency: Historical investment (1930s TVA, 1950s Western projects) created initial clustering. New dams tend to locate near existing infrastructure (shared transmission lines, management expertise, known hydrology), reinforcing clusters.
Comparison to Q4 purpose patterns: Irrigation + Hydroelectric + Flood Control dams cluster similarly (they follow drainages). Water Supply dams differ—they form isolated urban clusters (Phoenix, Denver) rather than regional systems. This suggests different management scales: irrigation/hydro are basin-scale; water supply is city-scale.

Conclusion: Dam attributes reveal genuine geographic structure. Neighboring hexagons have similar characteristics because they share hydrology, policy jurisdiction (river basins), and development history. This spatial dependence will be important for Q6 (LISA analysis) where we map hotspots explicitly.

section: Step 6.2 — Compute LISA for hexagon grid
text:
Step 6.2 — Compute LISA for hexagon grid

# Build neighbor matrix
W_hex <- st_touches(hexagon_clipped, sparse = FALSE) * 1
diag(W_hex) <- 0
W_hex_std <- W_hex / rowSums(W_hex)
W_hex_std[!is.finite(W_hex_std)] <- 0

# Extract dam counts and compute spatial lag
counts_hex <- hex_dams_cropped$n
lag_hex <- as.vector(W_hex_std %*% counts_hex)

# Standardize
z_hex <- scale(counts_hex)[, 1]
lag_z_hex <- scale(lag_hex)[, 1]

# Assign LISA quadrants — preserve geometry from hexagon_clipped
lisa_hex_attributes <- data.frame(
  n_dams = hex_dams_cropped$n,
  z = z_hex,
  lag_z = lag_z_hex,
  quadrant = case_when(
    z_hex > 0 & lag_z_hex > 0 ~ "HH (Hotspot)",
    z_hex < 0 & lag_z_hex < 0 ~ "LL (Coldspot)",
    z_hex > 0 & lag_z_hex < 0 ~ "HL (High-Low)",
    z_hex < 0 & lag_z_hex > 0 ~ "LH (Low-High)",
    TRUE ~ "Neutral"
  )
)

# Join attributes back to geometry
lisa_hex <- hexagon_clipped %>%
  bind_cols(lisa_hex_attributes)

section: Step 6.5 — Geographic Interpretation and Management Implications
text:
Step 6.5 — Geographic Interpretation and Management Implications
A+ Student Synthesis:
Geographic Hotspots (HH - High dam density with high-density neighbors):
The LISA map reveals three major HH hotspots:

Tennessee Valley Authority Region (Tennessee, Kentucky, Alabama, Mississippi): A contiguous HH cluster appears around the Tennessee River network. This represents the most iconic mid-20th-century U.S. water infrastructure system. TVA’s coordinated management of mainstem and tributary reservoirs created an archetypical multi-state basin. Management implication: This region demands coordinated interstate water policy. Spillway decisions in Kentucky affect downstream conditions across multiple states.
Colorado River Basin (Colorado, Utah, Arizona, Nevada, California): HH cells align with the mainstem and key tributary corridors. Older than TVA (early 20th-century large projects), but equally critical. The 1922 Colorado River Compact allocated water across 7 states + Mexico using wetter historical flow assumptions, now stressed by demand and climate change. Management implication: This region faces high coordination pressure as supply risk increases.
California Water System: Mixed HH/HL structure spans Sierra-fed storage through Central Valley transfer systems. This differs from purely riverline hotspots and reflects engineered coordination across linked but non-identical subsystems. Management implication: Operational failures can cascade across long distances where urban and agricultural users share storage and conveyance.

Geographic Coldspots (LL - Low dam density with low-density neighbors):
Coldspots occupy a large share of the domain, which reflects geography rather than policy failure:

Great Basin (Nevada, eastern California, Utah interior): Arid interior with minimal year-round flow. Dams here are for small irrigation, not power. Geography renders large infrastructure infeasible.
Mountain interiors (Montana, Idaho, interior Oregon): Steep terrain, low population, minimal water demand. Hydrology supports small craft dams, not major infrastructure.
Appalachian interior (eastern Kentucky, West Virginia): Historically coal-dependent economy; limited industrial water demand. TVA dams concentrate in River valleys; interior hills are sparse.

Management implication: Coldspots aren’t failures—they reflect natural resource limits. Policy should focus on HH hotspots where coordination matters; coldspots are self-managing due to scarcity.
Outliers (HL and LH tiles):
A subset of HL (high-count, low-lag) hexagons appear in the Southwest: - Elephant Butte Reservoir (Rio Grande): Isolated large dam in otherwise sparse region - Possible explanation: Historical project predating modern regional integration; or water imported from elsewhere (Colorado River aqueduct) - Management implication: These represent outlier projects—policy coordination might be inconsistent with neighboring regions
LH tiles (low-count surrounded by high-count) are present but more spatially scattered than HH/LL clusters. This suggests local transition zones and boundary effects rather than dominant regional anomalies.
Tessellation Robustness (MAUP at Local Scale):
Comparing Hexagon vs. County: - HH hotspot locations: Broad regions are similar (TVA, Colorado, California), but county boundaries fragment some continuous hotspot corridors visible in hexagons. - Quadrant counts: Counties typically produce different HH/LL totals because polygon size and shape vary dramatically across states. - Interpretation: The story is directionally consistent, but local detail is more MAUP-sensitive with counties due to administrative boundary effects.
This reinforces our Q3 recommendation: hexagons are better for process-based spatial structure, while counties are useful when decisions are made at administrative units. MAUP affects local pattern detail, not the core conclusion that dam clustering is real.
Q4 Hypothesis Revisited:
Prediction was: “Irrigation + Hydroelectric hotspots will dominate all-dams LISA; Flood Control creates secondary peaks in Mississippi Valley.”
Outcome: Confirmed. Irrigation dams concentrate in West (HH cluster in Colorado Basin, California). Hydroelectric dams concentrate in North/Northwest (Cascade Range) and South (Appalachians). Combined, they create Western hotspots visible in LISA. Flood Control dams are secondary (fewer total count) but cluster along Lower Mississippi—these appear as HL or embedded within broader HH regions. Hypothesis was mostly correct: tessellation scale resolved dams at basin level, not individual purpose; but clear geographic patterns emerged.
Management Implications:

Focus coordination on HH hotspots: TVA, Colorado River Compact, California Water Commission—existing multi-state bodies already operate at LISA hotspot boundaries. LISA analysis validates that these regions are genuinely integrated infrastructure systems requiring coordinated policy.
Don’t over-manage coldspots: Sparse dam regions (Great Basin, mountain interiors) are naturally stable. Policy efforts there have low ROI compared to hotspots where interdependencies are high.
Monitor outlier projects (HL tiles): Individual dams in sparse regions may have outsized impact on local water availability. Risk assessment should flag them.
Climate adaptation strategy: LISA shows current hotspots reflect 20th-century wet-period designs (Law of the River, 1922 Compact, TVA growth era). Climate change will shift hydrology—water availability may move away from current hotspot infrastructure. Future LISA analyses (5–10 years) could reveal whether new dams cluster in climate-resilient regions or entrench outdated infrastructure.

title: Lab 3: MAUP in Practice — Tessellations and Point-in-Polygon
text:
In this lab we will explore the impacts of tessellated surfaces and the modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP) using the National Dam Inventory maintained by the United States Army Corps of Engineers. The work requires writing reusable functions and careful consideration of feature aggregation/simplification, spatial joins, and data visualization. The end goal is to visualize the distribution of dams and their purposes across the country.
DISCLAIMER: This lab can be computationally intensive. For some steps you may be processing hundreds of millions of relations; run code chunk-by-chunk during development rather than knitting the whole document repeatedly. Your final knit may take a few minutes. Be proud — the report will summarize analyses over very large geometric relations.

This lab covers 4 main skills:

Tessellating surfaces to discretize space
Geometry simplification to expedite expensive intersections
Writing functions to automate repetitive reporting and mapping tasks
Point-in-polygon counts to aggregate point data



In addition to producing correct code and outputs, your submission should:

Justify methodological choices: Why did you choose a particular tessellation keep percentage for simplification? How did you balance computational efficiency with map detail?
Document performance impacts: Measure and report computation time and geometric accuracy changes resulting from simplification. How do results differ?
Apply spatial reasoning: Use spatial predicates (e.g., st_touches, st_contains) to identify and describe geometric relationships in the dam dataset that raw counts cannot reveal.
Compare across methods: When multiple tessellation approaches yield different clustering patterns, explain which pattern better supports real-world dam management decisions and why.
Connect to lecture: Explicitly cite the MAUP problem, simplification algorithms (Douglas-Peucker vs. Visvalingam), and spatial predicate definitions from week 3 lectures in your analysis.
